title: Blood Pressure Awareness at the Barangay
situation: Nurse Liza Dimaculangan works at a barangay health center in a rural municipality. Many residents have high blood pressure, but few come for regular check-ups. She meets the barangay captain, barangay health workers and a group of adult residents to plan a community health session on blood pressure control.

items.stem: The barangay captain, health workers and residents themselves meet with the nurse and decide which health problem to tackle first. Which principle of primary health care does this best illustrate?

options.label: A
options.text: Equity in access to services
options.why_not: Equity is about fair reach of services to all groups, not about residents deciding priorities.

options.label: B
options.text: Community participation

options.label: C
options.text: Intersectoral collaboration
options.why_not: This involves other sectors such as education or agriculture, which is not the cue here.

options.label: D
options.text: Use of appropriate technology
options.why_not: This concerns methods that are acceptable and affordable, not who sets priorities.

items.rationale: The decisive cue is that residents take part in identifying and prioritising their own health problem; this is community participation, a core principle of primary health care. Intersectoral collaboration is the strongest distractor, but it requires partner sectors beyond health, which the scenario does not describe.
items.rationale_simplified: When residents help choose and plan what to work on, that is community participation.

meta.competency: Applies principles of primary health care

items.stem: The nurse will teach a mixed group of adults about controlling high blood pressure. Which actions apply adult-learning principles? Select all that apply.
options: Ask participants what they already know and what they want to learn
Relate the content to their daily meals and work routines
Use only medical terms so the information stays accurate
Invite participants to share their own experiences
Keep the session as a one-way lecture to save time
Use the local language and simple pictures or demonstrations
items.rationale: Adults learn best when teaching builds on their experience, relates to real-life needs, and uses language and methods they understand. Medical jargon and a purely one-way lecture limit understanding and involvement, so they are poor choices.
items.rationale_simplified: Adults learn when teaching uses what they know, fits their daily life, and is easy to understand.

meta.competency: Plans and conducts community health teaching

items.stem: Choose the level of prevention that completes each statement.
items.text: Screening residents for high blood pressure to detect disease early is {{1}} prevention, while teaching healthy eating to residents who have no disease is {{2}} prevention.
items.rationale: Secondary prevention means early detection and prompt treatment, which is what screening does. Primary prevention means keeping disease from occurring in people who are well, as in health education for healthy people. Tertiary prevention limits disability and aids rehabilitation after disease is established.
items.rationale_simplified: Screening finds disease early (secondary); teaching well people to stay healthy is primary prevention.

meta.competency: Classifies health activities by level of prevention

items.stem: Select the parts of the nurse's post-session note that show the teaching objectives were NOT yet achieved.

segments.text: Twelve of fifteen participants named foods they should limit.
Three participants could not explain why medicines must be continued even when they feel well.
Most participants correctly showed the arm position for blood pressure measurement.
One participant said she will stop her tablets once she feels better.
Several participants thanked the nurse and asked for another session.

items.rationale: Learners who cannot explain why treatment continues, or who plan to stop medicine when symptoms disappear, have not met the objective on medicine adherence. Thanks and requests for another session show satisfaction, but they are not evidence of learning.
items.rationale_simplified: Look for what people cannot do or say correctly; being thankful does not prove they learned.

meta.competency: Evaluates learning outcomes of health teaching

items.stem: Which evaluation method best shows that participants can correctly check their own blood pressure at home?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask the group whether they understood the steps that were taught
options.why_not: Self-report of understanding does not confirm a skill.

options.label: B
options.text: Count how many people attended and stayed for the whole session
options.why_not: Attendance measures participation, not learning.

options.label: C
options.text: Give a written quiz on the definition and causes of hypertension
options.why_not: This tests knowledge of a definition, not the ability to perform the skill.

options.label: D
options.text: Have each participant perform it while the nurse observes

items.rationale: A psychomotor skill is best evaluated by return demonstration, in which the learner performs the procedure and the nurse observes accuracy. A written quiz tests cognitive recall only, and asking whether people understood often brings polite agreement even when errors remain.
items.rationale_simplified: To check a skill, watch the person do it.

meta.competency: Evaluates learning outcomes of health teaching

image_suggestion.description: Close-up of an adult seated with arm supported at heart level while a cuff is applied to the upper arm and a stethoscope is placed over the brachial artery.

title: Immunization Day at the Rural Health Unit
situation: Nurse Mario Santos conducts an immunization session at a rural health unit. Mrs. Gina Reyes brings her 3-month-old son for a scheduled vaccine. She says he has had a runny nose and a mild cough for two days but he is feeding well, is active and is not feverish. She is worried that he may not be allowed to receive the vaccine today.

items.stem: After screening, the nurse finds the baby active, feeding well and without fever. Which action is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Proceed with the scheduled vaccine and reassure the mother

options.label: B
options.text: Postpone the vaccine until the cough has completely cleared
options.why_not: A minor cold without fever is not a usual reason to delay and causes a missed opportunity.

options.label: C
options.text: Refer the infant to a physician for clearance first
options.why_not: Routine referral is unnecessary for a minor illness in a well-appearing infant.

options.label: D
options.text: Give a fever-reducing medicine to the baby before the injection
options.why_not: Routine pre-medication is not required and adds an unneeded step.

items.rationale: A well-appearing infant with only a mild cold and no fever can usually be vaccinated, so the nurse proceeds and reassures the mother. Delaying causes missed opportunities and leaves the child unprotected, which is the main weakness of the deferral option.
items.rationale_simplified: A baby who is well apart from a mild cold can still be vaccinated.

items.stem: The RHU nurse prepares for an outreach immunization session. Which practices help maintain the cold chain? Select all that apply.
options: Keep vaccines within the recommended temperature range
Record refrigerator temperature regularly
Store drinks and food in the vaccine refrigerator
Leave vaccines on the table during the whole session
Place vaccines in a cold box with ice packs during outreach
Open the refrigerator door often to check the vaccines
items.rationale: The cold chain keeps vaccines at the recommended temperature from storage to administration, so vaccines are kept in a proper refrigerator, temperatures are monitored, and vaccines travel in a cold box. Storing food, leaving vaccines out and opening the door often all expose vaccines to temperature changes.
items.rationale_simplified: Vaccines must stay cold the whole time, from the fridge to the child.

image_suggestion.description: A vaccine carrier or cold box packed with conditioned ice packs, vaccine vials and a thermometer, showing the arrangement of items inside.

items.stem: The mother asks what to expect after the injection. Which teaching is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Babies should show no reaction, so any fussiness or fever means the vaccine did not work
options.why_not: Mild reactions are common and do not mean the vaccine failed.

options.label: B
options.text: A fever after the injection is harmless, so there is no need to return even if the baby looks very ill
options.why_not: Danger signs need prompt attention; this advice is unsafe.

options.label: C
options.text: Mild soreness or fever may occur; return at once if the baby is very sleepy or has trouble breathing

options.label: D
options.text: Hold back breastfeeding for the rest of the day so the baby's stomach can settle
options.why_not: There is no need to stop breastfeeding after routine vaccination.

items.rationale: Parents should be told about common mild reactions and about warning signs that require prompt care, such as unusual drowsiness or breathing difficulty. Telling parents that no reaction occurs or that all fever is harmless is inaccurate and may delay care.
items.rationale_simplified: Tell the mother what is normal and which warning signs mean she must come back at once.

items.stem: Complete the statements about types of immunity.
items.text: Immunity gained when the body makes its own antibodies after a vaccine is {{1}} immunity, while antibodies passed from a mother to her baby through the placenta give {{2}} immunity.
items.rationale: A vaccine stimulates the person's own immune system, giving artificial active immunity. Antibodies that cross the placenta are received ready-made through a natural process, so this is natural passive immunity.
items.rationale_simplified: A vaccine makes the body produce its own protection; antibodies from the mother are borrowed protection.

items.stem: Place each nursing responsibility in the correct time of the immunization visit.

rows.text: Ask about a severe reaction to a previous dose
Check the expiry date of the vaccine
Observe the child for an immediate reaction
Record the vaccine, date and injection site
Advise the mother when to return for the next dose

items.rationale: Screening for contraindications and checking the vaccine are done before administration. Observation, documentation and giving return instructions follow administration so the mother has complete information and the record is accurate.
items.rationale_simplified: Check safety first; watch, record and give advice afterwards.

meta.competency: Carries out pre- and post-immunization responsibilities

title: Postpartum Home Visit
situation: Nurse Carlo Mendoza visits Mrs. Ana Villanueva, 28, four days after she delivered her second baby at the district hospital. Mrs. Villanueva says the baby has been feeding poorly since last night and seems unusually sleepy. She also has mild afterpains and describes her vaginal discharge as red-brown without odor. The house is clean and her older child is playing nearby.

items.stem: Select the findings in the nurse's home-visit note that need urgent attention.

segments.text: Mother reports red-brown lochia without foul odor.
Newborn has been feeding poorly since last night.
Newborn is hard to wake and feels limp when picked up.
Umbilical cord stump is dry with no redness.
Mother has mild afterpains; breasts are soft.
Older child is playing and appears well.

items.rationale: Poor feeding together with unusual sleepiness and limpness are newborn danger signs that may indicate serious infection or another grave illness. Red-brown lochia and mild afterpains are expected on the fourth postpartum day, so they are not the urgent concerns.
items.rationale_simplified: A newborn who feeds poorly and is hard to wake is in danger; the mother's findings are normal.

meta.competency: Recognises danger signs in the newborn

items.stem: Which action should the nurse take first for the newborn?

options.label: A
options.text: Advise the mother to breastfeed more often and review the baby again in two days
options.why_not: Delays care for a baby showing danger signs.

options.label: B
options.text: Advise giving sugar water by spoon at home until the baby becomes more awake
options.why_not: Gives no reliable benefit and risks aspiration; it is not a substitute for urgent care.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the baby warm and refer immediately to a facility that treats sick newborns

options.label: D
options.text: Finish the routine postpartum checklist first, then decide whether referral is needed
options.why_not: Completing routine tasks first delays urgent care.

items.rationale: A newborn who feeds poorly and is difficult to wake needs urgent assessment and care that cannot be provided at home, so the nurse keeps the baby warm and refers immediately. Completing the routine checklist or waiting for a revisit would delay treatment of a possibly life-threatening condition.
items.rationale_simplified: A sleepy newborn who will not feed needs to go to a facility now.

meta.competency: Prioritises care and referral for sick newborns

items.stem: Which findings are expected in the mother on the fourth day after a normal vaginal delivery? Select all that apply.
options: Mild afterpains, especially during breastfeeding
Lochia with a foul odor
A firm uterine fundus that is gradually descending
Lochia changing to a red-brown color
Soaking a pad quickly with passage of large clots
Severe headache with blurred vision
items.rationale: Afterpains, a firm descending fundus and lochia changing from bright red to red-brown are part of normal uterine involution. Foul-smelling lochia suggests infection, rapid soaking with large clots suggests hemorrhage, and severe headache with blurred vision is a danger sign requiring prompt care.
items.rationale_simplified: Mild cramps, a firm uterus and darker bleeding are normal; foul smell, heavy bleeding and severe headache are not.

meta.competency: Differentiates normal from abnormal postpartum findings

items.stem: Complete the description of good breastfeeding attachment.
items.text: A well-attached baby has the mouth {{1}} open and the lower lip turned {{2}}, with more areola visible above the mouth than below it.
items.rationale: Good attachment features a wide-open mouth, a lower lip that is turned outward, the chin touching the breast and more areola visible above than below. Good attachment allows effective milk transfer and prevents nipple pain.
items.rationale_simplified: A good latch has a wide mouth and an outward-turned lower lip.

image_suggestion.description: Mother breastfeeding a newborn showing the baby's mouth wide open around the areola, chin touching the breast and body turned toward the mother.

items.stem: Classify each newborn finding.

rows.text: Occasional sneezing and hiccups
Convulsions
Fast breathing with chest indrawing
Peeling of the skin on the hands and feet
Body feels very cold despite wrapping

items.rationale: Sneezing, hiccups and mild peeling of the skin are common and harmless in newborns. Convulsions, breathing difficulty with chest indrawing and persistent coldness are danger signs requiring prompt medical care.
items.rationale_simplified: Sneezing and peeling are normal; fits, hard breathing and being very cold are emergencies.

meta.competency: Differentiates normal and abnormal newborn findings

image_suggestion.description: A series of photographs of a newborn's skin, umbilical cord stump and eyes in different conditions, shown without captions so the learner must judge each.

title: Cluster of Fevers in Purok 3
situation: Nurse Joy Alcantara at a rural health unit is told by barangay health workers that five children in the same purok have had fever for two to three days within one week during the rainy season. Many households keep uncovered water drums, and old tires lie around the yards. One of the children, a 9-year-old, is brought in on the fourth day with fever, headache and body aches.

items.stem: What is the most appropriate first action of the nurse regarding the cluster of cases?

options.label: A
options.text: Advise families to treat fevers at home and report again after one month if it persists
options.why_not: This delays detection and response to a possible outbreak.

options.label: B
options.text: Wait for laboratory confirmation of every child before notifying anyone in authority
options.why_not: Prompt reporting should not wait for complete confirmation.

options.label: C
options.text: Begin fogging the whole barangay at once, before any other action is taken
options.why_not: Fogging alone is not the first or sole measure; it does not replace reporting and removing breeding sites.

options.label: D
options.text: Report the cluster to the surveillance unit and start collecting case details

items.rationale: Several similar illnesses in one area within a short time suggest a possible outbreak, so the nurse promptly notifies the surveillance unit and gathers information on cases. Waiting for full confirmation delays the response, and spraying without investigation does not address breeding sites.
items.rationale_simplified: Several similar cases close together should be reported quickly.

items.stem: Which household measures help reduce mosquito breeding and bites? Select all that apply.
options: Cover water storage containers tightly
Dispose of or turn over old tires and cans that collect rainwater
Change water in flower vases regularly
Use repellent and wear long sleeves during the day
Depend on a mosquito net at night to protect against daytime bites
Leave water containers uncovered for convenience
items.rationale: Mosquitoes that carry dengue breed in clean stored water and bite mostly during the day. Covering containers, removing water-collecting objects, changing water and using personal protection by day reduce the risk, whereas a night-only net does not protect against daytime biting.
items.rationale_simplified: Remove places where water collects and protect yourself from daytime bites.

image_suggestion.description: Photograph of household containers and areas where Aedes mosquitoes breed, such as water drums, used tires, flower vases and clogged gutters.

items.stem: Decide whether each finding in a child with suspected dengue can be managed with close home monitoring or needs urgent referral.

rows.text: Fever with mild body aches; drinking well and passing urine normally
Persistent vomiting; unable to keep fluids down
Severe abdominal pain
Bleeding from the gums or nose
Mild headache; alert, eating small meals and drinking fluids

items.rationale: A child who is alert, drinks well, passes urine and eats small meals may be monitored at home with clear return advice. Persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain and bleeding are warning signs of severe disease and need urgent medical evaluation.
items.rationale_simplified: A child who is alert, drinking and passing urine can stay home; vomiting, severe tummy pain or bleeding means go now.

meta.competency: Recognises warning signs of severe dengue

image_suggestion.description: Skin of a child's forearm showing a petechial rash and a tourniquet-test site, shown without a caption.

items.stem: Choose the correct words for the home care advice.
items.text: For fever the mother is advised to give {{1}} as ordered and to encourage plenty of {{2}}.
items.rationale: Paracetamol is the usual choice for fever in suspected dengue, whereas aspirin and other NSAIDs are avoided because they may increase bleeding risk. Adequate oral fluids help prevent dehydration, which is a main concern during the illness.
items.rationale_simplified: Use paracetamol, not aspirin, and give lots of fluids.

items.stem: A nurse trainee asks what disease surveillance means. Which is the best explanation?

options.label: A
options.text: A one-time survey of residents carried out after an outbreak has already ended
options.why_not: Surveillance is ongoing, not a single survey.

options.label: B
options.text: Ongoing, systematic collection and analysis of health data to guide public health action

options.label: C
options.text: Treating each sick person at the health center until he or she has recovered
options.why_not: Describes clinical care, not surveillance.

options.label: D
options.text: Spraying or cleaning the places where disease-carrying insects breed
options.why_not: This is a control measure, not surveillance.

items.rationale: Surveillance is the ongoing systematic collection, analysis and interpretation of health data, followed by use of the information for action. A single survey, case treatment and vector control are separate activities.
items.rationale_simplified: Surveillance means always watching the health data so action can be taken early.

title: Sanitation Survey in a Coastal Barangay
situation: Nurse Rosario Lim joins the rural health unit sanitary inspector in a sanitation survey of a coastal barangay. Some households share an open well that is near a pit latrine, a few families defecate in the open near the creek, and garbage is dumped near the water where children play. Several young children have had repeated episodes of watery stools.

items.stem: Which survey finding poses the greatest immediate risk of contaminating the shared drinking-water source?

options.label: A
options.text: A pit latrine dug close to the shared well

options.label: B
options.text: Chickens kept in fenced pens in the backyards
options.why_not: This is less likely to contaminate a protected well than a nearby latrine pit.

options.label: C
options.text: Dry leaves swept into a pile and burned each week
options.why_not: This is an air pollution issue, not a direct contaminant of the well.

options.label: D
options.text: Kitchen waste in a covered compost pit far from the well
options.why_not: A covered pit placed far from the well is an acceptable practice.

items.rationale: Human waste from a pit latrine close to a well can seep into the water and spread fecal-oral diseases such as diarrhea. The other options are lesser or acceptable practices, so the latrine location is the greatest risk.
items.rationale_simplified: A toilet pit near the well can pollute the drinking water.

items.stem: Which household practices help make drinking water safer? Select all that apply.
options: Bring water to a rolling boil and let it cool
Store treated water in a clean covered container
Use a clean dipper with a handle to get water
Dip cups directly into the storage container
Keep water in an uncovered pail for easy access
Wash hands with soap before handling drinking water
items.rationale: Boiling kills disease-causing organisms, and clean covered storage with a handled dipper prevents recontamination. Dipping cups and uncovered storage reintroduce germs, which cancels the benefit of treatment.
items.rationale_simplified: Treat the water, keep it covered, and never put hands or cups into it.

items.stem: Classify each household waste item.

rows.text: Vegetable peelings
Clean plastic bottles
Used batteries
Banana leaves
Broken thermometer containing mercury

items.rationale: Food and plant waste decays naturally and can be composted. Clean plastic can be reused or recycled, while batteries and mercury need special handling because they can poison people and the environment.
items.rationale_simplified: Plant waste rots, clean plastic can be reused, and batteries or mercury are dangerous.

image_suggestion.description: Set of colour-coded waste containers for segregation (biodegradable, recyclable, residual, hazardous) as used in community or health facility settings.

items.stem: Complete the statements about the nurse's role.
items.text: The nurse's main contribution to community sanitation is {{1}} and mobilizing residents, while coordinating with the {{2}} for inspection and enforcement.
items.rationale: Nurses educate and mobilize the community and coordinate with the sanitary inspector, who has the authority to inspect and enforce sanitation standards. Treating individuals alone does not address the environmental cause of illness.
items.rationale_simplified: The nurse teaches and organizes, and works with the sanitary inspector.

meta.topic: Role of the community health nurse

items.stem: A mother asks how to care for her child who has watery stools but is still alert and drinking. Which advice is best?

options.label: A
options.text: Stop all food and fluids for several hours so that the stomach can rest
options.why_not: Withholding fluids worsens dehydration.

options.label: B
options.text: Give plain water by itself until the stools become formed again
options.why_not: Plain water does not replace lost salts and food should continue.

options.label: C
options.text: Continue feeding and give oral rehydration solution as directed

options.label: D
options.text: Give an anti-diarrheal medicine that a neighbor used for her own child
options.why_not: Unprescribed medicines are not advised for children.

items.rationale: In diarrhea the priority is to replace fluid and salts with oral rehydration solution while continuing normal feeding. Withholding fluids or giving unprescribed anti-diarrheal drugs can be harmful.
items.rationale_simplified: Keep feeding and give oral rehydration fluid.

title: Reading the Municipal Health Data
situation: Nurse Rhea Bautista at the municipal health office is preparing the annual health report. The municipality has a mid-year population of 5,000. At the start of the year, 25 residents already had a chronic disease, and 15 more residents developed it during the year. There were 40 live births and 10 deaths during the year.

items.stem: Which measure counts only the new cases of a disease that develop in a population during a given period?

options.label: A
options.text: Prevalence rate
options.why_not: Includes both new and existing cases.

options.label: B
options.text: Case fatality rate
options.why_not: Measures deaths among those with the disease.

options.label: C
options.text: Crude death rate
options.why_not: Measures all deaths in the population, not new cases.

options.label: D
options.text: Incidence rate

items.rationale: Incidence reflects new cases occurring over a period and shows the risk of developing disease. Prevalence is the strongest distractor because it includes existing cases as well.
items.rationale_simplified: Incidence counts only the new cases.

items.stem: Which are appropriate uses of vital statistics in community health planning? Select all that apply.
options: Identifying groups at higher risk of illness or death
Deciding how to allocate limited health resources
Evaluating whether a health program is making a difference
Choosing the medication dose for an individual patient
Making a medical diagnosis for one client
Planning services based on the community's age groups
items.rationale: Vital statistics describe the health of populations, so they help identify risk groups, allocate resources, evaluate programs and plan services. They do not guide an individual's diagnosis or dosing.
items.rationale_simplified: Vital statistics help plan for groups, not treat one person.

image_suggestion.description: Population pyramid (age-sex distribution) for a developing-country municipality, with age bands on the vertical axis and males and females on opposite sides.

items.stem: The municipality has a mid-year population of 5,000 and recorded 40 live births in the year. What is the crude birth rate per 1,000 population?

options.label: A
options.why_not: This is the number of births, not a rate per 1,000.

options.label: C
options.why_not: Decimal misplaced; the result must be multiplied by 1,000.

options.label: D
options.why_not: Incorrect scaling of the calculation.

items.rationale: Crude birth rate is live births divided by mid-year population, multiplied by 1,000. Here, 40 divided by 5,000 is 0.008, and multiplying by 1,000 gives 8 per 1,000 population.
items.rationale_simplified: Divide births by population and multiply by 1,000.

items.stem: Classify each measure.

rows.text: Incidence rate
Crude death rate
Infant mortality rate
General fertility rate
Attack rate

items.rationale: Morbidity measures describe illness, mortality measures describe deaths, and fertility measures describe births. Attack rate is a morbidity measure used during outbreaks.
items.rationale_simplified: Illness measures are morbidity, death measures are mortality, birth measures are fertility.

items.stem: Complete the definition.
items.text: Epidemiology is the study of the distribution and {{1}} of health-related conditions in populations, and the application of this study to {{2}} health problems.
items.rationale: Epidemiology studies how diseases are distributed and what factors determine them, then applies findings to prevent and control health problems.
items.rationale_simplified: Epidemiology studies who gets sick and why, to control problems.

title: First Home Visit to the Cruz Family
situation: Nurse Ben Ocampo will make a first home visit to the Cruz family of six: the parents, three children and Lola, 68, who has hypertension and was recently seen at the rural health unit. The nurse brings the public health bag and plans to assess the family's health situation and ability to care for Lola.

items.stem: Before the first home visit to the Cruz family, what should the nurse do first?

options.label: A
options.text: Review the family record and set the objectives of the visit

options.label: B
options.text: Write a care plan for each family member before meeting any of them
options.why_not: Care plans must be based on assessment done with the family.

options.label: C
options.text: Examine every family member for illness as soon as the nurse arrives
options.why_not: Examination belongs to the visit proper and follows preparation and the family's consent.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask the barangay captain to decide what the objectives of the visit will be
options.why_not: The nurse and family set objectives, not an outside person.

items.rationale: Preparation comes first: reviewing the available family record and defining the purpose of the visit makes the visit focused and efficient. Writing care plans before meeting the family skips assessment, and examining everyone on arrival is done during the visit, not before preparing for it.
items.rationale_simplified: Prepare and set goals before the visit.

image_suggestion.description: Family genogram or family tree of a six-member household with three generations, using standard symbols, with no health problems marked.

items.stem: Which actions follow correct bag technique during the home visit? Select all that apply.
options: Wash hands before and after caring for the client
Place the bag on a clean, lined surface
Set the bag on the floor beside the family's pets
Keep clean and contaminated items separate in the bag
Return used items to the bag without cleaning them
Clean the bag after the visit
items.rationale: Bag technique prevents cross-infection between the nurse, the bag and the families visited. Hand hygiene, a clean lined surface, separating clean from contaminated items and cleaning the bag achieve this, while floors and unclean items return germs to the bag.
items.rationale_simplified: Keep the bag clean and the items separate to avoid spreading germs.

image_suggestion.description: Public health nurse's bag laid open on a clean surface with a newspaper or paper lining, showing the usual contents arranged for use.

items.stem: Match each family action to the family health task it shows.

rows.text: The mother notices Lola's swollen feet and says something is wrong
The family agrees to bring Lola to the health center instead of waiting
Her daughter gives her medicines on time and prepares low-salt meals
The family covers water containers and cleans the surroundings weekly
The family registers Lola with the rural health unit and attends its monthly hypertension clinic

items.rationale: The five family health tasks are recognizing a health problem, deciding on action, caring for a sick member, maintaining a healthful environment and using community resources. Each action here fits one task.
items.rationale_simplified: The tasks are notice, decide, care, keep the home healthy and use outside help.

items.stem: Choose the correct family health problem classification.
items.text: A family member with diagnosed hypertension is a {{1}}, while a family whose child is about to start school is facing a {{2}}.
items.rationale: A health deficit exists when a health problem is present, such as a diagnosed illness. A foreseeable crisis is an expected stressful event in family life, such as a child's entry to school.
items.rationale_simplified: An existing illness is a deficit; an expected life change is a foreseeable crisis.

items.stem: During the visit the nurse learns that the family cannot afford all of Lola's medicines. Which action best reflects family-centered care?

options.label: A
options.text: Tell them to buy all of the prescribed medicines, regardless of the cost to the family
options.why_not: Ignores the family's situation.

options.label: B
options.text: Discuss the family's priorities and link them to available resources

options.label: C
options.text: Shorten the visit and note the problem to raise at the next staff report
options.why_not: Does not solve the problem.

options.label: D
options.text: Give them some of your own money so they can buy the medicines
options.why_not: Not sustainable and outside professional boundaries.

items.rationale: Family-centered care works with the family's circumstances, so the nurse explores priorities and links them to resources such as the rural health unit. Giving personal money is not sustainable and blurs professional boundaries.
items.rationale_simplified: Work with the family and connect them to available help.

title: Evacuation Center After the Typhoon
situation: After a strong typhoon caused flooding, Nurse Maricel Navarro is assigned to an evacuation center in a school gymnasium. Hundreds of families are crowded together, toilets are shared, and many residents have lost their homes. Among them are infants, pregnant women and older adults with chronic illnesses.

items.stem: What should the nurse do first on arrival at the evacuation center?

options.label: A
options.text: Start group health teaching about handwashing for the families present
options.why_not: Teaching comes after urgent needs are identified.

options.label: B
options.text: Begin detailed long-term follow-up records for each family in the center
options.why_not: Detailed records are not the first priority.

options.label: C
options.text: Do a rapid assessment of urgent health needs, hazards, water and toilets

options.label: D
options.text: Start giving routine vaccines to every evacuee who is present in the center
options.why_not: Not a first-line response without assessment of needs.

items.rationale: Early in a disaster response the nurse assesses urgent health needs and environmental risks so that resources are directed to the most pressing problems. Teaching and records follow once life-threatening needs are addressed.
items.rationale_simplified: First find out the most urgent needs and hazards.

meta.competency: Performs rapid assessment in a disaster

items.stem: Which groups are especially vulnerable in the evacuation center and need priority attention? Select all that apply.
options: Infants and young children
Pregnant women
Older adults
Persons with disabilities
Healthy young adult volunteers
Residents with no health problems
items.rationale: Children, pregnant women, older adults and persons with disabilities are more affected by disrupted care, crowding and limited resources, so they receive priority attention. Healthy adults are generally able to meet their own needs.
items.rationale_simplified: Those who depend on others or are at higher risk need attention first.

items.stem: Select the two findings in the rapid assessment note that need the most urgent attention.

segments.text: A pregnant woman reports regular painful contractions.
Two men have minor scratches on their forearms.
A toddler is lethargic with sunken eyes after repeated watery stools.
Volunteers are sorting donated clothes.
A boy says he is bored.

items.rationale: A woman in labor and a lethargic toddler with signs of dehydration have potentially life-threatening needs. Minor scratches and boredom are lower priority, and the sorting of clothes is not a clinical finding.
items.rationale_simplified: Labor and a lethargic dehydrated toddler are most urgent.

items.stem: Classify each activity by disaster phase.

rows.text: Conducting evacuation drills with the barangay
Providing first aid at the evacuation center clinic
Checking and stocking emergency supply kits
Counseling survivors who remain stressed after returning home
Rehabilitating contaminated water sources

items.rationale: Preparedness activities are done before a disaster, response activities during or immediately after, and recovery activities restore health and normal life afterward.
items.rationale_simplified: Before is preparedness, during is response, after is recovery.

image_suggestion.description: Cycle diagram of the disaster management phases (mitigation, preparedness, response, recovery).

items.stem: A mother sits quietly crying after losing her home. Which response is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Tell her to be strong and stop crying for the sake of her children
options.why_not: Dismisses feelings.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask her to describe in detail everything that happened during the typhoon
options.why_not: May increase distress.

options.label: C
options.text: Leave her alone for now and check on her again after a few days
options.why_not: Withdrawal may increase isolation.

options.label: D
options.text: Stay near her, offer water, and listen if she wishes to talk

items.rationale: Psychological first aid offers calm presence, basic comfort and the choice to talk, without forcing disclosure. Pressuring her or dismissing feelings can worsen distress.
items.rationale_simplified: Be with her calmly and listen if she wants to talk.

title: Admission and progress in labor
situation: Maria Santos, 28 years old, G2P1, is admitted to the labor room of a district hospital at term. She reports regular, increasingly strong contractions and says the first baby was born vaginally. Her husband Ramon stays at the bedside. The nurse is responsible for her care during the next several hours.

items.stem: On admission, which action should the nurse do first?

options.label: A
options.text: Prepare the delivery table and call the family to the labor room
options.why_not: Premature; birth readiness depends on assessment findings first.

options.label: B
options.text: Assess her vital signs, contraction pattern and fetal heart rate

options.label: C
options.text: Give a large meal so she has energy for labor
options.why_not: Food in labor is not routinely encouraged and nothing here shows she needs it; assessment comes first.

options.label: D
options.text: Insert an indwelling urinary catheter for comfort
options.why_not: Unnecessary invasive procedure with no assessed need.

items.rationale: Assessment of the mother and fetus comes before routine interventions. The nurse needs baseline vital signs, the contraction pattern and the fetal heart rate to judge maternal and fetal well-being and to decide what to do next. Preparing for birth or doing procedures without data is premature.
items.rationale_simplified: Check the mother and the baby first, then decide what to do.

meta.tos_content_area: Care of the mother during labor and delivery
meta.competency: Initial assessment of the woman in labor

image_suggestion.description: Blank WHO partograph chart showing cervical dilatation, descent, fetal heart rate, contractions and alert and action lines.

items.stem: Maria is in active labor. Which supportive nursing measures are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Encourage position changes and walking if there are no contraindications
Remind her to empty her bladder regularly
Teach breathing and relaxation techniques and coach her during contractions
Stay with her and encourage her husband to give support
Instruct her to hold her breath and push with every contraction from now on
Keep her flat on her back until the baby is born
items.rationale: Position changes, a regularly emptied bladder, relaxation techniques and continuous supportive presence all promote comfort and progress. Pushing before the woman is ready exhausts her and can cause cervical swelling, and lying flat on the back can reduce blood flow to the uterus and fetus.
items.rationale_simplified: Help her move, void, relax and feel supported. Do not make her push early or lie flat.

meta.tos_content_area: Care of the mother during labor and delivery
meta.competency: Supportive care in the first stage of labor

items.stem: For each description, select the stage of labor it best describes.

rows.text: From full cervical dilation until the baby is born
From the birth of the baby until the placenta is delivered
From onset of regular contractions until the cervix is fully dilated
The first hours after delivery of the placenta, when bleeding and fundus are closely watched

items.rationale: Stages are defined by landmarks: the first ends at full dilation, the second at birth of the baby, the third at delivery of the placenta, and the fourth is the early recovery period. Mixing up the second and third stages is the common error because both involve delivery of something.
items.rationale_simplified: Each stage ends at a landmark: full dilation, baby born, placenta out, then recovery.

meta.tos_content_area: Care of the mother during labor and delivery

image_suggestion.description: Diagram of the stages of labor showing cervical dilatation and effacement, descent of the fetal head and delivery of the placenta.

items.stem: Choose the words that complete the nursing response to a woman in labor.
items.text: Maria says she has a strong urge to bear down and the perineum is bulging. The nurse should {{1}} and prepare for {{2}}.

choices: inform the birth attendant right away
ask her to cross her legs

items.rationale: A strong involuntary urge to bear down with a bulging perineum signals that birth is near. The nurse stays with the woman, informs the birth attendant at once and prepares the equipment. Delaying the report or asking her to resist the urge is unsafe.
items.rationale_simplified: Bearing down plus a bulging perineum means birth is close, so call the attendant now.

meta.tos_content_area: Care of the mother during labor and delivery
meta.competency: Recognizing the second stage of labor

items.stem: During a strong contraction Maria says, "I cannot do this anymore, I want to go home." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?

options.label: A
options.text: "Do not be silly, you already have a child and know exactly what you are supposed to do by now."
options.why_not: Dismisses her feelings and belittles her.

options.label: B
options.text: "Try to be calm and quiet, because your husband is watching you and he is getting worried."
options.why_not: Shifts focus to others and does not acknowledge her distress.

options.label: C
options.text: "You cannot go home now because you are already far along, so please stop saying that."
options.why_not: Confrontational and closes communication.

options.label: D
options.text: "This is a hard part of labor, and many women feel this way. I will stay right here with you."

items.rationale: Acknowledging the feeling, giving realistic reassurance and staying present supports the woman and keeps communication open. The other responses dismiss, deflect or reprimand. Strong self-doubt is common late in the first stage and is not a reason to argue with her.
items.rationale_simplified: Accept her feelings, reassure her honestly and stay with her.

meta.tos_content_area: Care of the mother during labor and delivery

title: Watching the fetal heart rate
situation: Rosario Dela Cruz, 24 years old, G1P0, is in active labor at a tertiary hospital. Labor is being augmented with an oxytocin infusion and the fetal monitor is in place. While reviewing the tracing, the nurse sees the fetal heart rate dipping after several contractions and returning to baseline slowly. Rosario is lying flat on her back.

items.stem: What is the nurse's best immediate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Encourage her to stay on her back and rest
options.why_not: The supine position may be contributing to reduced placental blood flow.

options.label: B
options.text: Document the pattern and recheck in an hour
options.why_not: Delay allows possible fetal compromise to continue.

options.label: C
options.text: Help Rosario turn to a side-lying position

options.label: D
options.text: Raise the oxytocin rate to finish labor sooner
options.why_not: Stronger contractions would further reduce placental blood flow.

items.rationale: Late-appearing decelerations suggest reduced blood flow to the placenta. A side-lying position relieves pressure of the uterus on the large vessels and is a quick, safe first step. Increasing oxytocin makes contractions stronger and worsens the problem, and waiting delays recognition of fetal compromise.
items.rationale_simplified: Turning her to her side helps blood reach the baby, so do it first.

meta.topic: Fetal heart rate monitoring and interpretation
meta.competency: Responding to a nonreassuring fetal heart rate

image_suggestion.description: Cardiotocography (CTG) strip showing fetal heart rate above and uterine contractions below, with a repeated dip in the fetal heart rate that begins after the peak of each contraction and returns late to baseline.

items.stem: Read the nurse's chart note. Select the findings that need prompt attention.

segments.text: 0900: Primigravida in active labor, oxytocin infusion running.
Baseline fetal heart rate is within the expected range.
Repeated late decelerations follow the contractions.
Variability is absent.
Mother is lying flat on her back.
Contractions are occurring regularly.
Mother says she is tired but has no other complaint.

items.rationale: Repeated late decelerations and absent variability are nonreassuring, and the supine position and ongoing oxytocin are contributing factors the nurse can act on. A baseline in the expected range is reassuring on its own, but it does not cancel the other findings.
items.rationale_simplified: Late dips, no variability and lying flat are the worrying parts.

meta.topic: Fetal heart rate monitoring and interpretation

items.stem: Which nursing actions are appropriate for this tracing? Select all that apply.
options: Stop or hold the oxytocin infusion according to protocol
Notify the physician or midwife of the findings
Check her blood pressure and watch for overly frequent contractions
Continue to observe the tracing closely
Increase the oxytocin infusion so labor is faster
Remove the monitor so she can walk around
items.rationale: Stopping or holding oxytocin, reporting to the provider, checking maternal vital signs and the contraction pattern, and close observation aim to restore placental blood flow and let the provider decide on further management. Increasing oxytocin or removing monitoring would harm or hide a possibly compromised fetus.
items.rationale_simplified: Stop the oxytocin, report, check her vital signs and contractions, and keep watching.

meta.topic: Fetal heart rate monitoring and interpretation

items.stem: Classify each fetal monitoring finding.

rows.text: Accelerations of the heart rate with fetal movement
Repeated late decelerations after contractions
Absent variability together with recurring decelerations
Moderate variability of the baseline

items.rationale: Accelerations with movement and moderate variability indicate a well-oxygenated fetus with an intact nervous system. Late decelerations and absent variability with decelerations point to inadequate oxygen reaching the fetus and must be reported promptly.
items.rationale_simplified: Accelerations and normal variability are good signs; late dips and flat tracing are not.

meta.topic: Fetal heart rate monitoring and interpretation

image_suggestion.description: Three paired fetal heart rate and contraction tracings illustrating early, variable and late decelerations, with the relationship to the contraction marked.

items.stem: Choose the words that complete the explanation the nurse gives to Rosario.
items.text: Lying on your {{1}} improves {{2}} to the placenta because the weight of the uterus is moved off the large blood vessels.
items.rationale: A side-lying position keeps the heavy uterus from compressing the large vessels, which improves blood flow to the placenta and fetus. The explanation also lets the woman cooperate with the position change.
items.rationale_simplified: Lying on your side lets more blood reach the baby.

title: Warning signs late in pregnancy
situation: Lourdes Reyes, 22 years old, G1P0 at about 34 weeks, goes to the rural health unit for her prenatal visit. She says she has had a headache for two days that does not go away with rest, and her face and hands look puffy. The nurse measures a blood pressure higher than her earlier visits and finds protein in her urine.

items.stem: Which findings should the nurse watch for because they suggest the condition is worsening? Select all that apply.
options: Persistent severe headache
Blurred vision or seeing spots
Pain in the upper abdomen
Sudden increase in swelling of the face and hands
Very little urine output
Mild backache after a long day of standing
Occasional mild tightening of the abdomen without pain
items.rationale: Severe headache, visual changes, epigastric pain, rapid swelling and falling urine output are signs of worsening hypertension in pregnancy and impending seizures. Mild backache and painless occasional tightening are common pregnancy discomforts and do not point to this complication.
items.rationale_simplified: Headache, blurred vision, upper belly pain, fast swelling and little urine are warning signs.

meta.tos_content_area: Care of the mother with high-risk pregnancy
meta.competency: Recognizing warning signs of worsening hypertension in pregnancy

items.stem: What is the most appropriate nursing action at the rural health unit?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep her side-lying and rested, and arrange urgent referral to a hospital with a companion

options.label: B
options.text: Send her home to rest in bed and return to the health unit at her next scheduled prenatal visit
options.why_not: Delays care for a potentially life-threatening condition.

options.label: C
options.text: Advise her to take a pain reliever for the headache and go back to her usual work this week
options.why_not: Treats a symptom and ignores the underlying risk.

options.label: D
options.text: Tell her to reduce her fluids and salt at home and return to the health unit next week
options.why_not: Home advice alone is inadequate; she needs prompt evaluation.

items.rationale: Headache with raised blood pressure and protein in the urine in late pregnancy signals a serious hypertensive disorder that can progress to seizures. The nurse keeps her quiet and safe and arranges prompt transfer to a facility that can manage it. Sending her home or advising only symptom relief leaves the risk untreated.
items.rationale_simplified: These signs can become dangerous quickly, so she needs urgent hospital care.

meta.tos_content_area: Care of the mother with high-risk pregnancy
meta.competency: Prioritising referral for a high-risk pregnancy

items.stem: Lourdes is admitted and magnesium sulfate is started. Which finding would require the nurse to stop the infusion and notify the physician?

options.label: A
options.text: Feeling warm and flushed
options.why_not: Warmth is a common, expected effect.

options.label: B
options.text: A calm, restful demeanor
options.why_not: Calmness is a desired effect.

options.label: C
options.text: Fetal movement felt after meals
options.why_not: Normal and reassuring.

options.label: D
options.text: Absent deep tendon reflexes

items.rationale: Loss of deep tendon reflexes, a falling respiratory rate and reduced urine output are early signs of magnesium toxicity. Warmth and flushing are expected, and calm rest is the goal. The nurse should stop the infusion, stay with the patient and report, following the facility protocol.
items.rationale_simplified: No reflexes means too much magnesium, so stop and report.

meta.tos_content_area: Care of the mother with high-risk pregnancy

image_suggestion.description: Technique for testing the patellar (knee-jerk) deep tendon reflex with a reflex hammer in a client lying or sitting with the knee relaxed.

items.stem: Select whether each seizure-precaution measure is appropriate or should be avoided.

rows.text: Keep the room quiet with low lighting
Keep side rails padded and up, with suction and oxygen at hand
Allow many visitors to talk and stimulate her
Leave her alone for long periods without checking

items.rationale: Stimulation can trigger a seizure, so the environment is kept calm. Padded rails, suction and oxygen prepare for an emergency, and frequent observation is required. Leaving her alone or allowing many visitors increases risk.
items.rationale_simplified: Keep her calm and safe with equipment ready, and do not leave her alone.

meta.tos_content_area: Care of the mother with high-risk pregnancy

items.stem: Choose the words to complete the health teaching to Lourdes and her family.
items.text: The condition usually resolves after {{1}}, and monitoring must continue {{2}} because seizures can still occur.

choices: birth of the baby and placenta

items.rationale: Delivery of the baby and placenta is the definitive treatment, but the risk of seizures does not end at birth, so assessment continues after delivery. Bed rest and diet may support care but do not resolve the condition.
items.rationale_simplified: Birth treats it, but the mother still needs close watching after delivery.

meta.tos_content_area: Care of the mother with high-risk pregnancy
meta.competency: Teaching about hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

title: Bleeding after birth
situation: Ana Villanueva, 30 years old, G3P3, gave birth vaginally to a healthy baby two hours ago and is in the recovery area of a district hospital. On assessment the nurse finds the fundus soft and pushed to the right of the abdomen, and a perineal pad that is soaked within a short time. Ana looks pale and restless.

items.stem: What should the nurse do first about Ana's soft, displaced fundus?

options.label: A
options.text: Apply a heating pad over the lower abdomen for comfort
options.why_not: Heat does not firm the uterus and may increase bleeding.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Ana to sit up and eat a full meal at once
options.why_not: Does not address bleeding and may worsen it.

options.label: C
options.text: Change the pad and reassess her again in two hours
options.why_not: Delay in a woman who is actively bleeding.

options.label: D
options.text: Massage the fundus gently until it becomes firm

items.rationale: A soft, displaced fundus with heavy bleeding suggests uterine atony, often with a full bladder pushing the uterus aside. Gentle fundal massage helps the uterus contract and compress open vessels, and the nurse also calls for help and then assists her to empty her bladder. Heat, feeding or waiting do not address the cause.
items.rationale_simplified: A soft womb causes bleeding, so massage it until firm.

image_suggestion.description: Postpartum nurse performing fundal massage with one hand cupping the fundus above the symphysis pubis while supporting the lower uterine segment with the other hand.

items.stem: Read the postpartum note. Select the findings that suggest hemorrhage and need action.

segments.text: Two hours after a normal vaginal birth.
Fundus soft and boggy, displaced to the right.
Bladder palpable above the symphysis.
Perineal pad saturated in a short time.
Mother pale and restless.
Perineum clean with mild swelling.
Newborn rooming-in and sleeping.

items.rationale: A boggy displaced fundus, a full bladder preventing contraction, rapid pad saturation and pallor with restlessness are signs of significant blood loss. Mild perineal swelling is common after birth and is not the concern here.
items.rationale_simplified: Soft womb, full bladder, soaked pad and pale restless mother point to bleeding.

items.stem: After the fundus becomes firm, which nursing actions should continue? Select all that apply.
options: Assist Ana to empty her bladder
Monitor vital signs and level of consciousness
Notify the physician or midwife of the bleeding
Keep a record of pad use and fundal checks
Stop assessing because the fundus is firm
Restrict all fluids
items.rationale: A full bladder prevents the uterus from staying contracted, so voiding is encouraged. Frequent monitoring and reporting detect ongoing blood loss early and guide treatment, and accurate records support decisions. A firm fundus does not mean the risk has passed, and fluids are not routinely restricted.
items.rationale_simplified: Keep watching, help her pass urine, report and write it down.

image_suggestion.description: Diagram showing the expected height of the uterine fundus relative to the umbilicus and symphysis pubis from delivery through the first postpartum days.

items.stem: Match each finding to its most likely cause of postpartum bleeding.

rows.text: Boggy fundus with heavy bleeding
Firm fundus with a continuous trickle of bright-red blood
Missing portion of the placenta on inspection
Soft uterus after a very long labor

items.rationale: A soft uterus is atony, which is common after prolonged labor. A firm fundus with persistent bright-red bleeding suggests trauma to the genital tract, and an incomplete placenta suggests retained tissue.
items.rationale_simplified: Soft womb means atony; firm womb with steady bleeding means a tear; missing placenta means retained tissue.

items.stem: Before discharge, which instruction about warning signs should the nurse give Ana?

options.label: A
options.text: Expect some heavy bleeding and clots and wait for the next check-up
options.why_not: Heavy bleeding and clots are not routine and need prompt evaluation.

options.label: B
options.text: Report sudden heavy bleeding, large clots, fever or foul-smelling discharge

options.label: C
options.text: Bleeding that becomes heavier with activity is a normal part of recovery and needs no action
options.why_not: Increasing heavy bleeding is not safe to dismiss.

options.label: D
options.text: Foul-smelling lochia is common after birth and needs no action
options.why_not: Foul odor suggests infection.

items.rationale: Women should know to report sudden heavy bleeding, large clots, fever, abdominal pain or foul-smelling discharge because they may indicate hemorrhage or infection. Dismissing these signs delays care.
items.rationale_simplified: Tell her to go back to the hospital for heavy bleeding, clots, fever or bad smell.

title: First hour with the newborn
situation: Jessa Mendoza, 25 years old, has just delivered a term baby girl at a rural health unit. The baby is crying strongly, breathing well and moving actively. Jessa says she wants to breastfeed. The nurse assists with the immediate care of the newborn.

items.stem: Which action should the nurse do immediately after birth?

options.label: A
options.text: Bathe the baby with warm water and wipe off the vernix right away
options.why_not: Early bathing causes heat loss and removes protective vernix.

options.label: B
options.text: Take the baby to the nursery for weighing and other routine procedures before the first feed
options.why_not: Separation interrupts bonding and warmth.

options.label: C
options.text: Dry the baby thoroughly and place her skin-to-skin on the mother's chest

options.label: D
options.text: Wrap her tightly in a blanket and give her to the waiting family
options.why_not: Delays skin-to-skin contact and does not keep warmth at the source.

items.rationale: Drying prevents heat loss, and skin-to-skin contact keeps the baby warm, supports bonding and stimulates early breastfeeding. Early bathing and separation from the mother are not recommended for a well newborn.
items.rationale_simplified: Dry her and put her on her mother's skin to stay warm.

meta.tos_content_area: Care of the newborn and breastfeeding mother

items.stem: Which actions belong to immediate newborn care for a well baby? Select all that apply.
options: Cover the baby and her head after drying
Maintain uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact
Delay clamping of the cord as advised by the protocol
Help the mother begin breastfeeding when the baby shows feeding cues
Give a bath right away
Separate the baby for routine procedures before the first feed
items.rationale: Keeping the baby warm, undisturbed skin-to-skin contact, delayed cord clamping and early breastfeeding support are core steps of early newborn care. Bathing and separation work against warmth and bonding.
items.rationale_simplified: Keep her warm and with her mother and start breastfeeding early.

meta.tos_content_area: Care of the newborn and breastfeeding mother

items.stem: The nurse observes Jessa breastfeeding. Which finding shows a good latch?

options.label: A
options.text: Baby's mouth is wide open, lips turned outward, chin against the breast

options.label: B
options.text: Baby's lips are pursed inward and only the nipple is taken into the mouth
options.why_not: Pursed lips with the nipple alone indicates shallow latch.

options.label: C
options.text: Baby's cheeks dimple with each suck and clicking sounds are heard during the feed
options.why_not: Cheek dimpling and clicking suggest poor attachment.

options.label: D
options.text: Mother feels increasing nipple pain that continues throughout the whole feed
options.why_not: Persistent pain suggests poor attachment.

items.rationale: A good latch has a wide mouth, flanged lips, the chin touching the breast and more areola visible above than below. Pain, clicking and cheek dimpling indicate poor attachment, which can lead to sore nipples and poor milk transfer.
items.rationale_simplified: A wide open mouth with lips turned out means a good latch.

meta.tos_content_area: Care of the newborn and breastfeeding mother

image_suggestion.description: Side-by-side drawings of a poor and a good breastfeeding latch (lips flanged, areola visible mostly above the mouth), without captions.

items.stem: Classify each observation during breastfeeding follow-up.

rows.text: Audible swallowing during feeds
Persistent nipple pain throughout each feed
Baby is content after feeds and has regular wet diapers
Baby sleeps after a few sucks and is hard to wake for feeds

items.rationale: Audible swallowing and a content baby with regular wet diapers indicate effective milk transfer. Ongoing pain or a baby too sleepy to feed suggests poor attachment or inadequate intake and needs more support.
items.rationale_simplified: Swallowing and wet diapers are good; pain or a sleepy baby who will not feed needs help.

meta.tos_content_area: Care of the newborn and breastfeeding mother

items.stem: Choose the words that complete the teaching to Jessa.
items.text: Breastfeeding should be started {{1}}, and the baby should be fed {{2}}.

choices: within the first hour after birth
only when the milk looks white
on demand, whenever she shows hunger cues

items.rationale: Early initiation promotes bonding, uterine contraction and milk supply, and feeding on demand lets the baby take the amount she needs. Strict schedules or routine supplements can reduce milk supply.
items.rationale_simplified: Start in the first hour and feed whenever the baby is hungry.

meta.tos_content_area: Care of the newborn and breastfeeding mother

title: A toddler who says no
situation: Carlo, 2 and a half years old, is brought by his mother Aling Nena to the barangay health center for a well-child visit. She says he refuses almost everything, shouts "No!", throws himself on the floor when upset, and climbs onto furniture. She also wants to know when to start toilet training.

items.stem: How should the nurse interpret Carlo's behavior?

options.label: A
options.text: It is a sign that the parents have failed to discipline him properly
options.why_not: Blames the parent without basis.

options.label: B
options.text: It is a normal sign of the toddler's search for independence

options.label: C
options.text: It is an early sign of a behavior disorder needing referral
options.why_not: Normal toddler behavior is not a disorder.

options.label: D
options.text: It means he is regressing and needs stricter limits
options.why_not: Regression is not indicated and strictness is not the answer.

items.rationale: Toddlers are in the stage of developing autonomy, and negativism and tantrums are expected expressions of it. Reassuring the parent and teaching consistent, safe limits is appropriate. There is no cue to suggest a disorder.
items.rationale_simplified: Saying no and tantrums are normal for toddlers learning to be independent.

meta.tos_content_area: Growth and development of the child

items.stem: Which safety teachings should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Store medicines and household cleaning products out of reach and locked
Never leave him alone near water
Keep small objects and hard foods that can cause choking away from him
Use gates on stairs and secure windows
Turn pot handles toward the back of the stove
Rely on him to remember the safety rules
items.rationale: Toddlers are curious, mobile and put things in their mouths, so safety depends on adult supervision and environmental control. A toddler cannot reliably remember or follow safety rules.
items.rationale_simplified: Keep dangerous things out of reach and always watch him.

meta.tos_content_area: Growth and development of the child

items.stem: Select the age group in which each behavior is typical.

rows.text: Parallel play next to other children
Imaginary friends and magical thinking
Team games with rules and rule-based thinking
Temper tantrums when told no

items.rationale: Toddlers play beside rather than with others and have tantrums as they test limits. Preschoolers use fantasy and imagination, while school-age children enjoy organized games with rules.
items.rationale_simplified: Toddlers play alongside others; preschoolers pretend; school-age children follow rules.

meta.tos_content_area: Growth and development of the child

image_suggestion.description: Chart or illustration of developmental milestones in toddlers, preschoolers and school-age children (motor, language, social).

items.stem: Carlo has a tantrum in the clinic. What should the nurse advise his mother to do?

options.label: A
options.text: Scold him loudly in front of other people and spank him to stop it
options.why_not: Physical punishment is harmful and ineffective.

options.label: B
options.text: Give him what he wants so that the tantrum ends quickly and he calms down
options.why_not: Reinforces tantrums.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep him safe, stay calm and nearby, and avoid giving in to the demand

options.label: D
options.text: Leave the room and ignore him completely until the crying has stopped
options.why_not: Leaving a toddler unattended is unsafe.

items.rationale: During a tantrum the child needs to stay safe, and the parent stays calm and consistent without rewarding the behavior. Punishing, giving in or leaving the child are not helpful.
items.rationale_simplified: Keep him safe, stay calm, and do not reward the tantrum.

meta.tos_content_area: Growth and development of the child

items.stem: Choose the words that complete the teaching about toilet training.
items.text: Toilet training should begin when the child shows {{1}}, and parents should {{2}} his successes.

choices: the same pace as his cousins

items.rationale: Readiness varies, so training starts when the child can control his muscles and shows interest, not at a set age. Positive reinforcement supports learning, while punishment can cause fear and delay.
items.rationale_simplified: Wait until he is ready and praise him when he does well.

meta.tos_content_area: Growth and development of the child

title: Immunisation visit
situation: Mrs. Liza Bautista brings her 2-month-old son Migo to the rural health unit for his scheduled immunisation. He is feeding well and active. His mother says he was a little fussy yesterday but has no fever today. This is her first baby and she is worried about side effects.

items.stem: Before giving the vaccine, what is the nurse's priority?

options.label: A
options.text: Give the vaccine first and ask the screening questions afterward to save time
options.why_not: Screening must come before administration.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask only whether he has fed today and whether he slept well during the night
options.why_not: Incomplete screening.

options.label: C
options.text: Instruct the mother to hold him still and skip explaining the procedure to her
options.why_not: Parents should be informed and consent to the procedure.

options.label: D
options.text: Screen for current illness and previous vaccine reactions, and check his record

items.rationale: Safe immunisation requires screening for contraindications such as acute illness and previous reactions, verifying the record, and explaining the procedure to the parent. Giving first and asking later is unsafe.
items.rationale_simplified: Always check for illness and past reactions before giving a vaccine.

items.stem: Which instructions should the nurse give to the mother? Select all that apply.
options: Mild fever, soreness at the site and fussiness can occur
Continue to feed the baby as usual
Report difficulty in breathing or swelling of the face
Keep the immunisation card and bring it on the next visit
Apply a hot herbal paste to the injection site
Withhold feeds for the rest of the day
items.rationale: Mothers should know the expected mild reactions, how to comfort the baby, which signs need urgent help and the importance of the record. Applying unproven substances to the site or withholding feeds is harmful or unnecessary.
items.rationale_simplified: Tell her what is normal, what is urgent, keep feeding and keep the card.

image_suggestion.description: Diagram of the anterolateral thigh of an infant showing the injection site for intramuscular vaccination.

items.stem: A few minutes after the injection, Migo's lips swell and he begins to wheeze. What is the nurse's first action?

options.label: A
options.text: Call for emergency help and maintain his airway while staying with him

options.label: B
options.text: Reassure the mother and tell her to observe the baby at home for the next day
options.why_not: Delays treatment of a possible severe allergic reaction.

options.label: C
options.text: Give him a feed to calm him and make him comfortable before anything else
options.why_not: Feeding may cause choking with respiratory distress.

options.label: D
options.text: Place him in a crib and finish documenting the vaccination first
options.why_not: Leaving him unattended is unsafe.

items.rationale: Swelling and wheezing soon after a vaccine suggest a severe allergic reaction, which is an emergency. The nurse stays with the infant, supports the airway and summons help immediately, which is also why infants are observed after vaccination.
items.rationale_simplified: Wheezing and swelling after a vaccine is an emergency, so get help and protect the airway.

meta.competency: Responding to an immediate vaccine reaction

items.stem: Classify each finding after immunisation.

rows.text: Tenderness at the injection site
Mild fussiness with a low-grade fever
Difficulty in breathing
Seizure
Prolonged, inconsolable high-pitched crying

items.rationale: Local tenderness and mild fussiness or low-grade fever are common and settle. Breathing difficulty, seizures and prolonged inconsolable crying are not expected and require urgent evaluation.
items.rationale_simplified: Soreness and mild fussiness are fine; trouble breathing, seizures or endless crying need help.

items.stem: Choose the words that complete the explanation to the mother.
items.text: A vaccine gives {{1}} immunity by stimulating the body to make {{2}} without causing the full disease.
items.rationale: Vaccines trigger the child's own immune system to produce antibodies and memory cells, which is active immunity. Passive immunity is borrowed from another source, such as the mother or a serum.
items.rationale_simplified: A vaccine teaches the body to make its own protection.

title: A child struggling to breathe
situation: Paolo Ramos, 4 years old, is brought to the emergency room of a district hospital by his father. He has a known history of asthma and has been coughing and breathing noisily since the evening. The father says he cannot finish a sentence without stopping to breathe.

items.stem: Read the assessment note. Select the findings that show respiratory distress.

segments.text: Child is sitting upright, leaning forward, using shoulder muscles to breathe.
Retractions between the ribs and under the ribcage.
Nasal flaring present.
Wheezing heard on breathing out.
Lips look bluish.
Temperature is normal.
Father reports he ate breakfast yesterday.

items.rationale: Use of accessory muscles, retractions, nasal flaring, wheeze and bluish lips show increased work of breathing and poor oxygenation. A normal temperature is useful but does not indicate the severity of distress.
items.rationale_simplified: Leaning forward, pulling in at the ribs, flaring nostrils, wheeze and blue lips show he is struggling.

meta.tos_content_area: Care of the child with respiratory disorders

items.stem: What is the nurse's priority action for Paolo right now?

options.label: A
options.text: Lay him flat on the bed to rest and keep the room quiet and dimly lit
options.why_not: Lying flat worsens breathing.

options.label: B
options.text: Offer a large drink and a snack to give him energy for the night
options.why_not: Risk of aspiration while in distress.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep him upright and comfortable, prepare oxygen and call the provider urgently

options.label: D
options.text: Take a complete, detailed history from the father before any treatment is begun
options.why_not: Treatment must not be delayed by prolonged history-taking.

items.rationale: A child in respiratory distress needs airway and breathing support first. An upright position eases breathing, oxygen is prepared and the provider is called without delay. History can be taken while care is given.
items.rationale_simplified: Sit him up, get oxygen ready and call the doctor now.

meta.tos_content_area: Care of the child with respiratory disorders

items.stem: Which findings suggest that Paolo is getting worse? Select all that apply.
options: Increasing restlessness followed by drowsiness
Bluish discoloration of lips
Worsening retractions
Inability to speak or feed
A very quiet chest with little air movement
Able to play and speak in full sentences
items.rationale: Drowsiness, cyanosis, deepening retractions, inability to talk and a silent chest are signs of fatigue and impending respiratory failure. Playing and speaking in full sentences show improvement.
items.rationale_simplified: Sleepiness, blue lips, harder breathing and a silent chest mean he is getting worse.

meta.tos_content_area: Care of the child with respiratory disorders

items.stem: Classify each sign of respiratory distress.

rows.text: Restlessness and anxiety
Mild flaring of the nostrils
Drowsiness and difficulty to arouse
Cyanosis

items.rationale: Anxiety and flaring appear early as the child tries to get more oxygen. Drowsiness and cyanosis occur when oxygen is critically low and indicate impending respiratory failure.
items.rationale_simplified: Restless and flaring early; sleepy and blue late.

meta.tos_content_area: Care of the child with respiratory disorders

image_suggestion.description: Photograph or drawing of a young child in respiratory distress at rest, showing chest wall movement and breathing pattern, without captions.

items.stem: Before discharge, which teaching for Paolo's father is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Stop all play and physical activity at home and at school to prevent attacks
options.why_not: Unnecessary restriction; activity can be adjusted.

options.label: B
options.text: Give his medicine only when he has a severe attack and stop it once he feels better
options.why_not: Controller therapy needs consistent use as prescribed.

options.label: C
options.text: Wait several hours at home before seeking help for any breathing difficulty
options.why_not: Delay is unsafe.

options.label: D
options.text: Keep the home free of smoke and dust, and follow the medication plan as prescribed

items.rationale: Reducing triggers such as smoke and dust and following the prescribed plan are the basis of asthma control. Total activity restriction, skipping prescribed therapy or delaying help is incorrect.
items.rationale_simplified: Remove triggers and give medicine as prescribed.

meta.tos_content_area: Care of the child with respiratory disorders

title: Diarrhea in a toddler
situation: Baby Ella Navarro, 18 months old, is brought to the rural health unit by her grandmother Lola Corazon. She has had watery stools and vomiting for two days. Her grandmother says she is very thirsty and irritable. The nurse starts the assessment.

items.stem: Which findings suggest dehydration? Select all that apply.
options: Sunken eyes
Dry mucous membranes
Decreased urine output
No tears when crying
Skin that returns slowly after being pinched
Puffy eyelids and moist mouth
items.rationale: Sunken eyes, dry mouth, reduced urine, absence of tears and slow skin return reflect fluid loss. Puffy eyelids with a moist mouth point to fluid excess, not loss.
items.rationale_simplified: Sunken eyes, dry mouth, little urine, no tears and slow skin return mean dehydration.

meta.tos_content_area: Care of the child with fluid and gastrointestinal problems

items.stem: Which measure best helps monitor Ella's fluid balance?

options.label: A
options.text: Observation of her appetite and how much she plays during the day
options.why_not: Not specific.

options.label: B
options.text: Intake and output records and weight compared with earlier weights

options.label: C
options.text: Asking the grandmother how tired the child looks each day and at night
options.why_not: Subjective and unreliable.

options.label: D
options.text: Checking her temperature several times a day with the same thermometer
options.why_not: Temperature does not measure fluid status.

items.rationale: Intake and output with weight trends are objective measures of fluid balance in a small child, because weight changes quickly with fluid loss or gain. The other options do not measure fluid status.
items.rationale_simplified: Measure what goes in and out, and her weight.

meta.tos_content_area: Care of the child with fluid and gastrointestinal problems
