items.rationale: Many ulcers are linked to NSAID use, so he should avoid self-medicating and consult his provider about safe pain control. Continuing irritants, stopping treatment early or drinking alcohol puts him at risk of re-bleeding.
items.rationale_simplified: He should check with his doctor before using any pain tablets.

title: Cirrhosis with increasing abdominal girth
situation: Mang Celso, 55, has alcohol-related cirrhosis and is admitted to a tertiary hospital with a swollen abdomen and leg swelling. The nurse observes yellow discoloration of the sclerae, small spider-like vessels on his chest and bruises on his forearms. His wife says he has been unusually sleepy during the day and awake at night.

items.stem: Which assessment findings are consistent with advanced liver disease? Select all that apply.
options: Jaundice of the skin and sclerae
Increasing abdominal girth
Spider-like vessels on the chest
Easy bruising
Brisk wound healing and well-developed muscles
Decreasing abdominal girth without any treatment
items.rationale: A failing liver causes bilirubin to accumulate (jaundice), fluid to collect in the abdomen (ascites), vascular changes such as spider angiomas, and reduced clotting factors leading to easy bruising. Good wound healing and muscle bulk would not be expected.
items.rationale_simplified: Yellow eyes, big belly, spider veins and easy bruising fit a failing liver.

image_suggestion.description: Photograph of an adult with yellow sclera, a distended abdomen and leg edema, shown without a caption.

items.stem: His wife reports he is sleeping by day and awake at night, and he is slow to answer. Which nursing action is most appropriate now?

options.label: A
options.text: Explain to his wife that daytime sleepiness is normal in a hospital ward.
options.why_not: This overlooks a possible serious change in mental status.

options.label: B
options.text: Offer a high-protein snack at once to improve his energy and alertness.
options.why_not: Nutrition does not address a neurologic change that needs assessment first.

options.label: C
options.text: Assess his orientation and level of consciousness and report the change.

options.label: D
options.text: Let him sleep and recheck him in the morning when he is more rested.
options.why_not: A delay could miss progressing encephalopathy.

items.rationale: A reversed sleep pattern and slowed responses in a client with cirrhosis may signal hepatic encephalopathy, caused by toxins such as ammonia affecting the brain. The nurse assesses neurologic status, keeps the client safe and reports early so treatment is not delayed.
items.rationale_simplified: New sleepiness and confusion in liver disease need to be checked and reported quickly.

items.stem: For each nursing measure, select whether it is appropriate or should be avoided for a client with cirrhosis.

rows.text: Use a soft toothbrush and an electric razor
Take over-the-counter medicines without asking the provider
Weigh daily and measure abdominal girth at the same time
Drink alcohol in small amounts
Elevate swollen legs when resting

items.rationale: Low clotting factors raise bleeding risk, so soft brushes and electric razors reduce injury. Daily weight and girth measurements track fluid accumulation. The damaged liver cannot safely handle alcohol or many medicines, so these are avoided unless approved.
items.rationale_simplified: Prevent bleeding, track fluid, and avoid alcohol and unapproved medicines.

items.stem: Mang Celso has generalized itching and scratches until his skin is broken. Which nursing measure is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Wash with hot water and strong soap so the skin is thoroughly clean.
options.why_not: Heat and harsh soap worsen dryness and itching.

options.label: B
options.text: Let him scratch lightly with his fingers, which relieves the itch.
options.why_not: Scratching damages skin and raises infection risk.

options.label: C
options.text: Cover the itchy areas with plastic wrap to keep the skin moist.
options.why_not: Occlusion can trap heat and moisture and irritate the skin.

options.label: D
options.text: Keep nails short, use cool bathing and a gentle non-drying skin product.

items.rationale: Itching in liver disease is thought to be related to retained bile products. Short nails, cool bathing and gentle moisturizing reduce skin damage, and avoiding irritants protects fragile skin. Hot water, harsh soap and scratching worsen the problem.
items.rationale_simplified: Keep nails short, bathe in cool water and use gentle skin products.

items.stem: Complete the statements about the liver's functions.
items.text: A damaged liver makes fewer {{1}}, which increases bleeding, and cannot clear {{2}}, which may affect the brain.
items.rationale: The liver produces most clotting factors, so impaired function increases bleeding and bruising. It also converts ammonia to a form that can be excreted, and when this fails ammonia accumulates and can cause confusion.
items.rationale_simplified: A weak liver means less clotting and a build-up of ammonia that affects the brain.

title: Falling urine output after surgery
situation: Gng. Linda, 68, is on her second day after emergency abdominal surgery with significant blood loss and low blood pressure in the operating room. She takes a pain reliever from the NSAID group at home. The nurse notes that her urine output has dropped markedly, her ankles are swollen and her weight has risen since admission.

items.stem: Select the risk factors and findings in this note that point to acute kidney injury.

segments.text: Emergency surgery with significant blood loss.
Low blood pressure during the operation.
Urine output markedly decreased.
Ankle swelling and weight gain.
Wound dressing dry and intact.
Takes pain reliever from the NSAID group.

items.rationale: Reduced blood flow to the kidneys from blood loss and low pressure is a common cause of acute kidney injury, regular NSAID use is a recognized risk factor, and falling urine output with fluid retention (edema, weight gain) shows the kidneys are not clearing fluid. The dry dressing is unrelated to kidney function.
items.rationale_simplified: Blood loss, low pressure, less urine and fluid gain point to the kidneys struggling.

meta.competency: Recognizes cues of acute kidney injury

items.stem: Which nursing action is most important in the care of Gng. Linda now?

options.label: A
options.text: Measure intake and output closely and report a continuing fall in urine.

options.label: B
options.text: Encourage her to drink as much water as she can to flush her kidneys.
options.why_not: Unlimited fluid can worsen overload in reduced kidney function.

options.label: C
options.text: Offer her usual NSAID for the surgical pain, since it worked well at home.
options.why_not: NSAIDs can further harm the kidneys.

options.label: D
options.text: Wait to notify the provider until her weight has risen even further.
options.why_not: Early reporting allows treatment before complications.

items.rationale: Accurate intake and output monitoring detects trends early and guides fluid management. Early reporting allows the cause to be found and treated. Free fluids and NSAIDs may worsen overload or kidney injury, and waiting delays care.
items.rationale_simplified: Track fluids in and out carefully and report falling urine.

meta.competency: Monitors fluid status in kidney injury

items.stem: For each cause, select the category of acute kidney injury it represents.

rows.text: Severe dehydration from vomiting and diarrhea
Enlarged prostate blocking the urethra
Kidney stones blocking both ureters
Heart failure with low cardiac output

items.rationale: Prerenal injury results from too little blood reaching the kidneys, as in dehydration or poor cardiac output. Postrenal injury results from obstruction of urine outflow, such as an enlarged prostate or stones in the ureters.
items.rationale_simplified: Prerenal means not enough blood flow; postrenal means urine cannot drain.

meta.competency: Classifies causes of acute kidney injury

items.stem: Which nursing actions are appropriate when caring for a client with acute kidney injury? Select all that apply.
options: Weigh the client at the same time each day with the same scale.
Review medicines with the provider for those that may harm the kidneys.
Observe for signs of fluid overload such as swelling and breathlessness.
Follow fluid and diet prescriptions carefully.
Give unlimited oral fluids to flush the kidneys.
Ignore changes in urine color and amount.
items.rationale: Daily weights, observation for overload, medicine review and adherence to prescribed fluids and diet support safe management of impaired kidney function. Unlimited fluids may cause overload, and ignoring urine changes delays recognition of deterioration.
items.rationale_simplified: Weigh daily, watch for fluid overload, review medicines and follow fluid orders.

meta.competency: Plans care for acute kidney injury

items.stem: Gng. Linda later requires hemodialysis through an arteriovenous fistula in her left arm, which was created years ago for another condition and is now in use. Which nursing action protects the access?

options.label: A
options.text: Use the left arm for routine blood pressure checks and blood draws.
options.why_not: Pressure and punctures can occlude or damage the fistula.

options.label: B
options.text: Check for a thrill and bruit and keep pressure and needles off that arm.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask her to carry heavy shopping bags with that arm to keep it strong.
options.why_not: Heavy loads and pressure can damage the access.

options.label: D
options.text: Wrap the arm snugly in a bandage to protect the fistula from knocks.
options.why_not: Constriction can reduce blood flow.

items.rationale: A functioning fistula has a palpable thrill and an audible bruit that confirm blood flow. Blood pressure cuffs, venipuncture, tight clothing, jewelry or heavy loads on the access arm can reduce flow or injure the fistula.
items.rationale_simplified: Feel and listen for the buzz of the fistula and keep pressure and needles off that arm.

image_suggestion.description: Photograph of a forearm with a surgically created arteriovenous fistula showing the raised, enlarged vein.

title: Sudden weakness at the market
situation: Mang Rodel, 70, with long-standing hypertension, collapses at a barangay market. A bystander says he was well 30 minutes ago. The responding nurse finds weakness of the right arm and leg, drooping of the right side of his face and slurred speech. He is awake but confused.

items.stem: Select the cues in the nurse's report that suggest a stroke.

segments.text: History of hypertension.
Right arm and leg weakness.
Right facial droop.
Slurred speech.
Well 30 minutes ago.
Collapsed while at the market.

items.rationale: One-sided weakness, facial droop and speech difficulty are classic stroke warning signs, and the time he was last known to be well is essential because treatment decisions depend on timing. Hypertension is a risk factor but not a sign of the current event.
items.rationale_simplified: Weakness on one side, a drooping face and slurred speech are stroke signs, and the time matters.

image_suggestion.description: Facial drooping on one side of the face and unequal arm raise in an older adult, as used in stroke recognition.

items.stem: Mang Rodel shows signs of a stroke at the market. Which action has the highest priority for the nurse?

options.label: A
options.text: Give him a drink of water to find out whether he can swallow.
options.why_not: Swallowing may be impaired, which risks aspiration.

options.label: B
options.text: Let him rest at the market stall and see if the weakness improves.
options.why_not: Delay reduces the chance of effective treatment.

options.label: C
options.text: Note when he was last known to be well and activate emergency transport.

options.label: D
options.text: Give aspirin from a bystander right away in case a blood clot caused the stroke.
options.why_not: The type of stroke is unknown until imaging, and medicines are given only on a provider's order.

items.rationale: A stroke is a time-critical emergency. Treatment options depend on when symptoms began or when the client was last well, so the time is recorded and emergency transport is activated without delay. Oral intake is avoided because swallowing may be impaired, and medicines are not given before the type of stroke is confirmed.
items.rationale_simplified: Stroke is an emergency, so note the time and get him to the hospital fast.

items.stem: While waiting for transport, which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Keep him on nothing by mouth.
Monitor his level of consciousness and breathing.
Keep him safe from falls and reassure him calmly.
Stay with him and note any change in his speech, strength or alertness.
Give him food to keep up his strength.
Ask him to stand and walk to test his strength.
items.rationale: Nothing by mouth protects against aspiration, and monitoring consciousness and breathing detects deterioration. Safety, calm reassurance and close observation for any change in speech, strength or alertness give the receiving team useful information. Food and walking are unsafe.
items.rationale_simplified: Nothing by mouth, watch him closely, keep him safe and calm, and avoid walking.

items.stem: In the hospital, Mang Rodel is monitored for rising intracranial pressure. Select whether each finding is an earlier or a later sign.

rows.text: Restlessness and subtle confusion
New or worsening headache
Slow heart rate with widening pulse pressure
Dilated pupil that does not react to light

items.rationale: Early rises in pressure cause subtle changes in alertness, behavior and headache. Late signs such as bradycardia with a widening pulse pressure and a fixed dilated pupil indicate brain compression and are emergencies. Changes in level of consciousness are often the earliest and most sensitive indicator.
items.rationale_simplified: Small changes in alertness come first; slow pulse and a fixed wide pupil come late.

meta.competency: Differentiates early and late ICP signs

items.stem: Which positioning of Mang Rodel best helps limit rising intracranial pressure?

options.label: A
options.text: Lying flat in bed with the head turned sharply to one side for comfort.
options.why_not: Neck twisting can impede venous drainage from the head.

options.label: B
options.text: Head-down position to increase blood flow to the brain.
options.why_not: This raises intracranial pressure.

options.label: C
options.text: Sitting upright with the hips and neck strongly flexed forward in a chair.
options.why_not: Strong flexion obstructs venous return from the head.

options.label: D
options.text: Head of the bed raised with the neck kept in neutral alignment.

items.rationale: Raising the head and keeping the neck neutral promotes venous drainage from the head and avoids increases in pressure. Head-down positions, neck twisting and marked flexion obstruct drainage and may raise pressure.
items.rationale_simplified: Raise the head and keep the neck straight so blood can drain.

meta.competency: Positions client with increased intracranial pressure

image_suggestion.description: Client lying in bed with the head of the bed raised about 30 degrees and the head and neck in neutral alignment.

title: A seizure on the ward
situation: Ana, 24, has epilepsy and is admitted to a district hospital after missing her anticonvulsant doses for several days. While sitting in a chair at her bedside, she suddenly stiffens, falls to the floor and begins rhythmic jerking of all limbs. A nurse is the first to reach her.

items.stem: Which action should the nurse take first during the seizure?

options.label: A
options.text: Hold her arms and legs down firmly to stop the jerking and keep her still.
options.why_not: Restraint can cause fractures and does not stop the seizure.

options.label: B
options.text: Protect her from injury by clearing the area and cushioning her head.

options.label: C
options.text: Place a folded spoon between her teeth so that she cannot bite her tongue.
options.why_not: Objects in the mouth can break teeth and obstruct the airway.

options.label: D
options.text: Pour cold water over her face to wake her from the seizure.
options.why_not: This does not stop a seizure and risks aspiration.

items.rationale: During a generalized seizure the nurse protects the client from harm, notes the time and characteristics, and never restrains her or places objects in her mouth. Once the jerking stops she is turned to the side to protect the airway.
items.rationale_simplified: Keep her safe from injury and do not hold her down or put anything in her mouth.

items.stem: Which observations should the nurse record about the seizure? Select all that apply.
options: Time the seizure started and how long it lasted
Body parts involved and the type of movements
Whether she lost consciousness
Her condition and orientation after the seizure
Any injury she sustained
Her opinion of the hospital food
items.rationale: Precise documentation of onset, duration, the pattern of movements, loss of consciousness, post-seizure state and injuries helps the team classify the seizure and adjust treatment. Her opinion of the food is unrelated.
items.rationale_simplified: Record when it started and ended, what happened, her awareness afterwards and any injury.

items.stem: Complete the statement about care after the jerking stops.
items.text: After the seizure the nurse should turn the client to the {{1}} position to protect the airway and then monitor her {{2}}.
items.rationale: A side-lying position lets saliva drain and reduces the risk of aspiration after a seizure. Breathing and level of consciousness are monitored until she is fully awake, because the post-ictal period can include drowsiness and confusion.
items.rationale_simplified: Turn her on her side and watch her breathing and alertness.

image_suggestion.description: Person in the recovery (lateral) position on their side with the upper leg bent and head tilted slightly back.

items.stem: The nurse teaches Ana's family how to help during a future seizure. Select whether each action is appropriate or should be avoided.

rows.text: Stay with her and note the time the seizure begins
Put a wallet or spoon in her mouth
Move hard or sharp objects away from her
Hold her arms and legs down
Turn her onto her side when the jerking stops

items.rationale: The family should keep her safe, time the event and place her in a side-lying position afterwards. Restraining her or putting objects in her mouth can cause injury and airway problems.
items.rationale_simplified: Stay, time it, clear the area and turn her on her side; never hold her down or put things in her mouth.

items.stem: Which situation after a seizure should the family be taught is an emergency requiring immediate medical help?

options.label: A
options.text: A seizure that does not stop, or repeated seizures without waking in between.

options.label: B
options.text: Drowsiness and mild confusion that gradually improve after a single short seizure.
options.why_not: Drowsiness after a seizure is common.

options.label: C
options.text: A mild headache and sore muscles after she has woken up from a seizure.
options.why_not: Headache and soreness after a seizure are common and are not an emergency.

options.label: D
options.text: Feeling very tired and wanting to sleep for a few hours after the seizure.
options.why_not: Fatigue is an expected post-ictal effect.

items.rationale: A prolonged seizure or repeated seizures without recovery (status epilepticus) can cause lasting brain injury and breathing problems and require emergency care. Drowsiness, headache and tiredness are common after a single seizure.
items.rationale_simplified: A seizure that will not stop, or one after another without waking, is an emergency.

title: Setting Limits on the Psychiatric Unit
situation: Ms. Liza Ocampo, 29, is admitted to the psychiatric unit of a tertiary hospital with unstable moods and frequent conflicts with her family. On her second day she repeatedly asks night-shift nurses for extra phone privileges and tells Nurse Ben, 'The other nurse said it was okay, so you should let me too.' She grows angry when he declines and says the staff 'only care about rules.' The unit's treatment plan limits phone use to scheduled times for all clients.

items.stem: Which response by Nurse Ben is most appropriate when Ms. Ocampo says another nurse allowed extra phone use?

options.label: A
options.text: Agree to one extra call this once so that she calms down and begins to trust him more
options.why_not: Gives in to pressure and undermines the treatment plan; reinforces manipulation.

options.label: B
options.text: State calmly and kindly that phone use follows the unit schedule for every client

options.label: C
options.text: Ask the other nurse in front of the client to say whether she really gave permission
options.why_not: Pulls the client into staff conflict and invites splitting.

options.label: D
options.text: Tell her that her request shows she is trying to control and manipulate all the staff
options.why_not: Interpretive and judgmental; likely to escalate anger.

items.rationale: The decisive cue is the attempt to play one nurse against another while the plan applies to all clients. A calm, brief, consistent statement of the limit keeps the plan intact and avoids a power struggle. Making an exception, even once, teaches the client that pressure works, and challenging her in front of others is more likely to escalate the situation.
items.rationale_simplified: Stay calm and say the same rule applies to everyone. Do not make exceptions.

items.stem: Which nursing actions support consistent limit setting for Ms. Ocampo? Select all that apply.
options: Discuss the limit and plan during the team handover so all staff respond the same way
Explain the limit in a calm, neutral tone without arguing
Decide privately each shift whether to allow exceptions
State the expected behavior and what will happen if the limit is crossed
Tell the client the limit is only for her because she is difficult
Document the client's behavior and the staff response objectively
items.rationale: Limits work when they are clear, applied the same way by every team member, and delivered without anger. Sharing the plan at handover and documenting objectively keep the team aligned. Individual shift-by-shift exceptions and labelling the client as difficult both weaken consistency and damage the therapeutic relationship.
items.rationale_simplified: Everyone on the team uses the same limit, says it calmly, and records what happened.

items.stem: For each nurse statement to Ms. Ocampo, select the communication category it best fits.

rows.text: You sound frustrated that you cannot call your sister right now.
Why did you shout at the other client this morning?
Don't worry, everything will turn out fine.
You seem upset about the visiting rules.

items.rationale: Reflecting names the feeling the client is expressing and invites her to say more. Asking 'why' pushes the client to defend herself and often sounds like criticism. Statements such as 'everything will turn out fine' offer reassurance the nurse cannot guarantee and shut down feelings.
items.rationale_simplified: Naming the feeling helps. 'Why' questions and empty promises do not.

items.stem: Complete the statement about setting limits by choosing the best word for each blank.
items.text: A limit names the {{1}} behavior, states the consequence of crossing it, and is applied {{2}} by every staff member.
items.rationale: A useful limit is specific so the client knows exactly what is not allowed, and it is applied consistently so that behavior is not reinforced by uneven responses. Vague limits or uneven enforcement give clients room to test the staff.
items.rationale_simplified: Say exactly what is not allowed and apply the rule the same way every time.

items.stem: Two days later, which client behavior best shows that the limit-setting plan is working?

options.label: A
options.text: She stops talking to the nurses so that there are no more disagreements with anyone
options.why_not: Withdrawal does not indicate improved coping.

options.label: B
options.text: She keeps asking different nurses the same question until one of them finally agrees
options.why_not: Continued splitting means the limit is not yet effective.

options.label: C
options.text: She calls her sister at the agreed time and says she felt frustrated but coped

options.label: D
options.text: She apologizes to every nurse on the unit and promises that she will never ask again
options.why_not: Overly eager promises are not evidence of learned coping.

items.rationale: Evidence of effectiveness is use of the agreed channel and an ability to name and manage frustration without manipulating staff. Withdrawal and excessive apology do not show new coping skills, and shopping the same request among nurses shows the pattern continues.
items.rationale_simplified: The plan works when she follows the schedule and handles frustration in a healthy way.

title: Recognizing Suicide Risk in Depression
situation: Mr. Arnel Dizon, 52, was admitted to a district hospital for dehydration. He lost his job three months ago and has been withdrawn, sleeping poorly and eating little. During the morning interview he says quietly, 'My family would be better off without me.' His wife mentions that he gave his watch and tools to his brother last week.

items.stem: What is the nurse's best next step after Mr. Dizon makes this statement?

options.label: A
options.text: Reassure him that his family loves him and that things will surely get better
options.why_not: False reassurance that closes the conversation.

options.label: B
options.text: Change the topic to his diet and fluids so that he does not dwell on his sadness
options.why_not: Avoids a potentially life-threatening cue.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask him directly whether he is thinking of suicide and whether he has a plan

options.label: D
options.text: Wait for the psychiatrist's next visit before discussing the statement with him
options.why_not: Delays assessment of immediate risk.

items.rationale: His statement and the giving away of belongings are warning signs, so the priority is to assess risk right away. Asking directly about suicidal thoughts and a plan does not plant the idea and opens the way to safety measures. Reassurance, changing the subject or waiting leaves a possible immediate risk unassessed.
items.rationale_simplified: Ask him straight out if he is thinking of suicide and whether he has a plan.

items.stem: Select the findings in the nursing note that most strongly suggest an increased risk of suicide.

segments.text: Admitted for dehydration;
lost his job three months ago;
said 'my family would be better off without me';
gave watch and tools to his brother;
states he has thought of hanging himself and knows where he would do it;
took half of his breakfast;
vital signs stable.

items.rationale: A statement of being a burden, giving away valued possessions and a stated method with a place are warning signs that indicate higher risk. Job loss is a stressor but not itself a sign of immediate intent, and eating half a meal is not a specific warning sign of suicide.
items.rationale_simplified: Being a burden, giving things away and having a plan are warning signs.

items.stem: Mr. Dizon tells the nurse that he has thought of hanging himself and knows where he would do it. Which actions should the nurse take to keep him safe? Select all that apply.
options: Place him in a room close to the nurses' station for close observation
Remove sharp objects, cords and other hazardous items from his area
Arrange for someone to stay with him continuously according to facility protocol
Promise to keep his thoughts secret if he agrees not to harm himself
Allow him to go to the bathroom alone with the door locked
Report the findings to the physician and document the assessment
items.rationale: Safety comes first: a high-risk client is kept in a visible area, hazards are removed and he is not left alone. The team must be informed, so the nurse cannot promise secrecy. Unsupervised time behind a locked door removes observation when he is most at risk.
items.rationale_simplified: Keep him in view, remove dangers, never leave him alone and tell the team.

items.stem: Complete the statement about a client who has a plan and the means to carry it out.
items.text: The client is at {{1}} risk, so the nurse should {{2}} and notify the physician.

choices: check on him when time allows

items.rationale: A specific plan with access to the means signals high risk, which calls for continuous presence and urgent communication with the physician. Checking only when time allows does not give protection against an impulsive act.
items.rationale_simplified: A plan plus the means means high risk. Stay with him and call the doctor.

items.stem: Several days later, which observation should concern the nurse most?

options.label: A
options.text: Mr. Dizon turns suddenly calm and cheerful and gives away more belongings

options.label: B
options.text: Mr. Dizon cries when his wife visits and talks at length about his lost job
options.why_not: Expressing feelings is expected and can be therapeutic.

options.label: C
options.text: Mr. Dizon eats a little more at each meal and drinks the fluids offered
options.why_not: Improving appetite suggests recovery.

options.label: D
options.text: Mr. Dizon asks when he may start joining the ward's morning exercise group
options.why_not: Interest in activities suggests engagement in treatment.

items.rationale: An abrupt, unexplained lift in mood after severe depression, together with giving away possessions, can mean that the client has decided to end his life and feels relief. The other findings are signs of expression of feelings or recovery and do not by themselves signal heightened danger.
items.rationale_simplified: A sudden calm after deep sadness, with giving things away, can be a danger sign.

title: Alcohol Withdrawal on a Medical Ward
situation: Mr. Danilo Reyes, 45, is on the medical ward of a district hospital two days after a fall in which he fractured his wrist. His wife says he drinks heavily every day. This morning he is sweating, his hands tremble, and he keeps picking at the bedsheets. He tells the nurse, 'There are insects crawling on the wall.' He is restless and his pulse feels fast.

items.stem: Which nursing action is the priority for Mr. Reyes at this time?

options.label: A
options.text: Reassure him that nothing is on the wall and let him rest alone in a quiet room
options.why_not: Does not protect from complications and leaves a confused client unobserved.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask about the exact amount of alcohol he drinks in order to confront his denial
options.why_not: Not a priority during acute withdrawal.

options.label: C
options.text: Encourage him to walk around the ward to use up his restless energy
options.why_not: Increases risk of falls and injury.

options.label: D
options.text: Monitor vital signs and mental status closely and start seizure precautions

items.rationale: Tremor, sweating, tachycardia and visual hallucinations after heavy drinking point to alcohol withdrawal, which can progress to seizures and delirium. The priority is close monitoring and safety measures. Confrontation and rest alone do not protect him, and walking about a confused client raises the risk of injury.
items.rationale_simplified: These are signs of alcohol withdrawal, so watch him closely and keep him safe.

items.stem: Which findings are consistent with alcohol withdrawal? Select all that apply.
options: Hand tremors
Excessive sweating
Fast heart rate
Visual hallucinations
Slow heart rate
Constricted pupils
Excessive sleepiness
items.rationale: Alcohol withdrawal is a state of nervous system overactivity: tremor, sweating, tachycardia, anxiety and hallucinations. Slow pulse, constricted pupils and heavy drowsiness suggest sedation or opioid effects, not withdrawal.
items.rationale_simplified: Withdrawal makes the body overactive: shaking, sweating, fast pulse and seeing things.

items.stem: For each nursing action, select whether it is appropriate or should be avoided for a client in alcohol withdrawal with hallucinations.

rows.text: Keep the room quiet and well lit
Argue with him that the insects are not real
Leave him alone for long periods
Use short, calm statements and orient him to reality
Place him in a bed near the nurses' station

items.rationale: A calm, well-lit, low-stimulation environment with frequent observation and simple reality orientation lowers fear and risk. Arguing with the hallucination increases agitation, and leaving a confused client alone for long periods risks injury.
items.rationale_simplified: Keep things calm, simple and close to staff. Do not argue or leave him alone.

items.stem: Complete the statement about care for a client with long-term heavy alcohol use.
items.text: These clients are at risk of deficiency of vitamin {{1}}, so supplementation may be ordered, and the nurse should {{2}} vital signs and mental status.
items.rationale: Chronic heavy drinking commonly leads to thiamine deficiency, which is why supplementation is typically ordered. Withdrawal can change quickly, so vital signs and mental status are monitored frequently rather than once per shift.
items.rationale_simplified: Heavy drinkers often lack vitamin B1. Check vital signs and mental status often.

items.stem: After recovery, Mr. Reyes says, 'I can quit anytime. I do not have a problem.' Which response is most therapeutic?

options.label: A
options.text: You are in denial, and you will end up with serious liver disease if you carry on
options.why_not: Confrontational and labeling.

options.label: B
options.text: You had a fall and withdrawal symptoms this week. What do you make of that?

options.label: C
options.text: If you do not stop drinking, your wife will probably leave you someday
options.why_not: Threatening; damages trust.

options.label: D
options.text: Many people drink in this way; it is nothing to be ashamed of, so do not worry
options.why_not: Minimizes the problem.

items.rationale: A nonjudgmental statement of observed facts followed by an open question invites reflection without attacking the defense of denial. Labeling, threats and minimizing either provoke defensiveness or reinforce denial.
items.rationale_simplified: State what you saw in a calm way and ask what he thinks about it.

title: Consent Before Surgery
situation: Mrs. Teresita Bautista, 67, is scheduled for abdominal surgery at a tertiary hospital the next morning. When Nurse Ana checks the chart, she finds the consent form already signed. Mrs. Bautista says quietly, 'I signed because the doctor was in a hurry, but I do not really know what they will do or what could go wrong.' Her son is at the bedside and says she should simply go ahead.

items.stem: What should Nurse Ana do first?

options.label: A
options.text: Inform the surgeon that the client has questions and needs an explanation

options.label: B
options.text: Explain the risks of the operation herself, since she has already read the chart
options.why_not: Giving the full explanation of the procedure is the physician's role.

options.label: C
options.text: Go ahead with the surgery preparations because the form is already signed
options.why_not: A signature does not show understanding.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask her son to explain the operation and its risks to her instead
options.why_not: The son cannot replace the physician's explanation.

items.rationale: Valid consent requires understanding, and the explanation of the procedure, risks, benefits and alternatives belongs to the physician who will perform it. The nurse acts as the client's advocate by relaying the concern so the explanation is given. A signature alone does not prove she understood.
items.rationale_simplified: The doctor must explain the surgery. The nurse tells the doctor she has questions.

image_suggestion.description: Specimen informed-consent form for surgery with blank signature and witness lines and standard sections, as used in a hospital.

items.stem: Which are essential elements of valid informed consent? Select all that apply.
options: The client has the capacity to decide
The decision is made voluntarily without pressure
The client receives information on risks, benefits and alternatives
The information is given in language the client understands
A signed form is enough even if the client does not understand
The client's relatives can overrule a competent adult's decision
items.rationale: Consent is valid when the client is competent, free from pressure, and adequately informed in understandable terms. A signature without understanding is only paper, and a competent adult's decision is not overruled by relatives.
items.rationale_simplified: Consent needs a capable, willing and well-informed client who understands.

items.stem: Select the bioethical principle that best matches each action.

rows.text: Respecting a competent client's decision to refuse a procedure
Giving pain relief to promote the client's comfort and well-being
Checking the identification band to avoid giving a treatment to the wrong client
Giving the same quality of care regardless of ability to pay

items.rationale: Autonomy is the right to self-determination, beneficence is doing good, nonmaleficence is avoiding harm, and justice is fairness in giving care. Each action matches the principle that is its main purpose.
items.rationale_simplified: Autonomy is choice, beneficence is doing good, nonmaleficence is avoiding harm, justice is fairness.

items.stem: Complete the statement about the nurse's role in consent.
items.text: The responsibility for explaining the procedure belongs to the {{1}} who will perform it, while the nurse may be asked to {{2}} the client's signature.
items.rationale: The professional performing the procedure explains it. The nurse's usual role is to witness, where facility practice asks for it, that the client signed voluntarily, and to advocate when the client appears not to understand. A nurse cannot sign for a competent adult.
items.rationale_simplified: The doctor explains. The nurse may witness the signing and speak up for the client.

items.stem: Mrs. Bautista says, 'My son says I must go ahead, but I am not sure.' Which response by the nurse best respects her autonomy?

options.label: A
options.text: Your son knows what is best for you, so you should trust his advice here
options.why_not: Undermines a competent adult's right to decide.

options.label: B
options.text: The surgery is needed, so it is better for everyone if you simply agree
options.why_not: Pressures the client.

options.label: C
options.text: The decision is yours; let us make sure you have the information you need

options.label: D
options.text: If you refuse the operation, the doctor will refuse to treat you ever again
options.why_not: Threatening and untrue.

items.rationale: A competent adult has the right to make her own decision, including refusing treatment. The nurse supports this by ensuring she is informed and free to choose. Pressure from family or staff, or threats, violate her autonomy.
items.rationale_simplified: She decides for herself. The nurse makes sure she has the information she needs.

title: Privacy and Negligence on the Ward
situation: Nurse Mara works on a medical ward of a tertiary hospital. A man who says he is a cousin of Mr. Santos, a client with a new diagnosis, asks her at the nurses' station what illness Mr. Santos has. Later she sees a coworker take a photo of another client's wound to send to a group chat. During the same shift a nurse gives a medication to a client without checking the allergy band and the client develops a rash and breathing difficulty.

items.stem: What is Nurse Mara's best response to the visitor who asks about Mr. Santos's diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Tell him the diagnosis because relatives usually have the right to know
options.why_not: Relatives do not have an automatic right; consent is needed.

options.label: B
options.text: Give a general hint about the illness so that he can prepare himself
options.why_not: Still discloses information.

options.label: C
options.text: Say politely that she cannot share health details without Mr. Santos's consent

options.label: D
options.text: Ask him to read the chart himself so that she does not have to say it aloud
options.why_not: Exposes the record to an unauthorized person.

items.rationale: Health information belongs to the client and is shared only with his consent or for care purposes. The nurse protects confidentiality by declining politely, and she may offer to ask Mr. Santos whether he wishes to share it. Hints and letting the visitor see the chart are still disclosures.
items.rationale_simplified: Health information is private. Ask the client before telling anyone.

items.stem: Which actions breach client confidentiality or privacy? Select all that apply.
options: Posting a photo of a client's wound in a group chat
Discussing a client's condition with colleagues in the elevator
Leaving the open chart on the counter where visitors can read it
Giving a complete report to the oncoming nurse caring for the client
Documenting care in the client's chart
Consulting the treating physician about the client's condition
items.rationale: Information must be shared only with those directly involved in the client's care and for care purposes. Photos on social groups, public conversations and unattended charts expose information to people with no need to know. Handover, documentation and consulting the treating physician are legitimate care activities.
items.rationale_simplified: Only share information with the people who need it for care, and in private places.

items.stem: The medication incident may amount to negligence. Match each fact with the element of negligence it shows.

rows.text: The nurse was assigned to care for the client that shift
The nurse did not check the allergy band before giving the drug
The reaction would not have happened if the drug had not been given
The client needed extra treatment and a longer stay

items.rationale: Negligence requires a duty owed, a breach of the standard of care, harm caused by the breach, and actual damages. Failure to perform a basic safety check is the breach; the extra treatment is the damage.
items.rationale_simplified: Negligence needs a duty, a mistake, the mistake causing harm, and real harm.

items.stem: Complete the statement about professional liability.
items.text: Failure to give the care that a reasonably prudent nurse would give is {{1}}, and when this is done by a professional in the course of practice it is called {{2}}.
items.rationale: Negligence is failing to act as a reasonably prudent person would; for a professional acting in the course of practice, it is termed malpractice. Battery, libel, slander and assault are different torts.
items.rationale_simplified: Not giving expected care is negligence. For professionals it is called malpractice.

items.stem: After the medication reaction, which action should the nurse who gave the drug take first?

options.label: A
options.text: Write in the client's chart that an incident report has been filed
options.why_not: Incident reports are not mentioned in the chart.

options.label: B
options.text: Wait to see whether the reaction settles before telling anyone about it
options.why_not: Delays treatment.

options.label: C
options.text: Correct the order in the record so that the error does not show
options.why_not: Altering records is improper and unethical.

options.label: D
options.text: Assess and stabilize the client and notify the physician right away

items.rationale: Client safety comes first: assess, call for help and notify the physician so treatment can start. Documentation of facts and an incident report follow through proper channels. Hiding the error or delaying disclosure harms the client and adds professional liability.
items.rationale_simplified: Protect the client first, then tell the doctor and report honestly.

image_suggestion.description: Blank medication incident report form with fields for date, time, drug, dose, client and actions taken.

title: Delegation and Priorities on a Surgical Ward
situation: Nurse Hazel is the team leader on a surgical ward of a provincial hospital. Her team includes Nurse Jun, a staff nurse, and Mang Ruel, a nursing attendant. Hazel's clients include a stable man who needs help with a bath, a woman scheduled for discharge teaching, a man who returned from surgery two hours ago, and a woman with a new surgical dressing. Midway through the shift Jun and Mang Ruel argue loudly in the corridor about who should transfer a client.

items.stem: Which task is most appropriate for Nurse Hazel to delegate to Mang Ruel?

options.label: A
options.text: Assisting a stable client with his bath and personal hygiene

options.label: B
options.text: Assessing the surgical dressing for possible signs of infection
options.why_not: Assessment cannot be delegated to unlicensed staff.

options.label: C
options.text: Teaching the woman about home care and medicines before discharge
options.why_not: Teaching requires nursing judgment.

options.label: D
options.text: Evaluating the postoperative client's response to pain relief
options.why_not: Evaluation belongs to the nurse.

items.rationale: Routine, predictable tasks for stable clients, such as bathing, may be delegated to unlicensed personnel. Assessment, teaching and evaluation require nursing judgment and remain with the nurse.
items.rationale_simplified: Simple care for a stable client can go to the attendant. Assessing, teaching and evaluating cannot.

image_suggestion.description: Organisation chart of a surgical ward nursing team showing the head nurse, team leader, staff nurses and nursing attendants and lines of authority.

items.stem: Which activities should Nurse Hazel NOT delegate to the nursing attendant? Select all that apply.
options: Initial assessment of the newly returned postoperative client
Discharge teaching
Interpreting a change in a client's condition
Helping a stable client eat his meal
Taking a stable client's routine vital signs
Assisting a stable client to the toilet
items.rationale: Assessment, teaching and interpretation of data call for nursing judgment and cannot be delegated to unlicensed personnel. Feeding, routine measurements and toileting for stable clients are acceptable tasks if the nurse reviews the results and supervises.
items.rationale_simplified: Thinking, assessing and teaching stay with the nurse. Routine help can be delegated.

items.stem: The postoperative client now reports sudden chest pain and shortness of breath. Which client should Nurse Hazel see first?

options.label: A
options.text: The woman who is waiting for her discharge teaching to begin
options.why_not: Not urgent.

options.label: B
options.text: The postoperative man with chest pain and breathlessness

options.label: C
options.text: The man who is waiting for assistance with his bath
options.why_not: Not urgent.

options.label: D
options.text: The woman who would like a new dressing applied for her comfort
options.why_not: Not urgent.

items.rationale: Sudden chest pain and breathlessness after surgery may signal a life-threatening complication, such as a clot in the lung. Using the airway, breathing and circulation priority, he is assessed first. The other tasks can wait or be delegated.
items.rationale_simplified: Chest pain and trouble breathing come first.

items.stem: Match each situation to the conflict resolution strategy it shows.

rows.text: The nurses meet, discuss the transfer problem and agree on a plan that meets both needs
Two nurses want the same weekend off and each gets one of the two days
A nurse stays away from a coworker to escape the disagreement
A nurse gives in to a coworker's demand even though she disagrees

items.rationale: Collaboration seeks a solution that satisfies both sides. Compromise gives each side partial satisfaction. Avoidance sidesteps the issue and accommodation yields to the other person.
items.rationale_simplified: Collaboration solves it together. Compromise splits it. Avoidance steps away. Accommodation gives in.

items.stem: Complete the statement about delegation.
items.text: Responsibility for a task may be delegated, but {{1}} for the outcome stays with the delegating nurse, who must also provide {{2}}.

choices: a written waiver from the client
a copy of the unit schedule

items.rationale: The delegating nurse remains accountable for outcomes, so she must choose the right task and person, give clear directions, supervise and evaluate. Delegation never ends the nurse's accountability.
items.rationale_simplified: You can hand over the task but not the accountability. Supervise and check.

title: Road Crash Casualties in the ED
situation: A passenger bus collides with a truck near a town, and four casualties arrive at the emergency department of a district hospital at about the same time. Nurse Paolo is the triage nurse. A man in his thirties was pulled from the wreckage; he is unresponsive, with gurgling breaths and blood in his mouth. A woman has a stable-looking forearm fracture and is alert. A young man with a bruised wrist is walking and talking. Another person is anxious and shouting loudly but has only minor scrapes.

items.stem: During the primary survey of the unresponsive man, what is the first priority?

options.label: A
options.text: Take a full crash history from the bus conductor
options.why_not: History comes later.

options.label: B
options.text: Splint the injured limbs before doing anything else
options.why_not: Not a first priority.

options.label: C
options.text: Check the pupils and record a neurologic score right away
options.why_not: Comes after airway is secured.

options.label: D
options.text: Open and clear the airway while keeping the neck protected

items.rationale: The primary survey follows life-threatening priorities, and an obstructed airway is the first. Gurgling and blood in the mouth need immediate clearing and opening, with the neck protected because of the mechanism of injury. History, splinting and pupil checks follow once airway and breathing are secured.
items.rationale_simplified: Airway first, and protect the neck.

image_suggestion.description: Rescuer performing a jaw-thrust manoeuvre on a supine trauma casualty with cervical spine protection.

items.stem: Select the findings in the triage note that indicate a threatened airway needing immediate intervention.

segments.text: Male, about 30, pulled from the wrecked bus.
Unresponsive to voice.
Gurgling sounds with each breath.
Blood pooling in the mouth.
Radial pulse present.
Bruise on the left forearm.

items.rationale: Unresponsiveness, gurgling and blood in the mouth indicate a threatened airway that needs immediate suctioning and opening. A palpable radial pulse and a forearm bruise are relevant to later assessment but do not show airway compromise.
items.rationale_simplified: Gurgling, blood in the mouth and being unresponsive mean the airway is in danger.

items.stem: Assign each casualty to the triage category that best fits.

rows.text: Unresponsive man with obstructed breathing that improves when the airway is opened
Alert woman with a closed forearm fracture and stable breathing
Young man who is walking with a bruised wrist
Anxious person with small scrapes

items.rationale: Immediate means life-threatening problems that can be reversed with prompt care. Delayed injuries are significant but stable and can wait safely. Minor injuries need only simple care and can wait longest.
items.rationale_simplified: Life-threatening and fixable is immediate. Stable but serious is delayed. Small injuries are minor.

image_suggestion.description: Triage tags with four colour categories (red, yellow, green, black) and a simple START triage flow chart, as used in multiple-casualty events.

items.stem: Which principles apply to triage during a multiple-casualty event? Select all that apply.
options: Casualties are sorted by urgency and chance of benefit from care
The triage category is reassessed as conditions change
The aim is the greatest good for the greatest number
Casualties are treated in the order in which they arrive
The loudest casualty is treated first
Triage is done once and need not be repeated
items.rationale: Triage sorts by urgency and likelihood of benefit, aims to do the most good for the most people and is repeated because conditions change. Order of arrival, noise level and a single assessment ignore clinical need.
items.rationale_simplified: Treat by urgent need, not by who comes first or shouts loudest, and reassess.

items.stem: After suctioning and opening the airway, which finding best shows that the intervention was effective?

options.label: A
options.text: The man remains unresponsive and the gurgling sounds are unchanged
options.why_not: Shows the problem persists.

options.label: B
options.text: The chest rises equally with each quiet, unlabored breath

options.label: C
options.text: Blood continues to flow from the mouth with every breath he takes
options.why_not: Shows persisting obstruction risk.

options.label: D
options.text: The nurse sees fewer onlookers gathered around the stretcher
options.why_not: Irrelevant to airway status.

items.rationale: The goal is a clear airway with effective breathing, shown by quiet unobstructed breaths and equal chest rise. Persisting gurgling or continued bleeding in the mouth means the airway is still threatened, and the crowd size is irrelevant.
items.rationale_simplified: A good result is quiet breathing with the chest rising evenly.
